profile.name: AgentMail
profile.what_it_does: API-first email provider that gives AI agents their own inboxes — "Gmail, but for agents." Programmatic inbox creation, send/receive with threading, webhooks + WebSockets for real-time events, IMAP, custom domains with DKIM/SPF/DMARC, semantic "Agent Search" over an inbox, LLM-driven auto-labeling and structured extraction, multi-tenant "Pods" for platform builders, and "Outposts" BYOC deployment. Python/TypeScript SDKs plus an MCP server. Positions the inbox as an agent's identity and persistent record. Their own published customers include AISDR, Balance, Lanesurf, Locus, Pancake, Cofounder, DoAnything, Eragon, Junior, Browser Use, AgentCard and Dossium; distribution/integration partners include Vercel, Telnyx, Clay, LiveKit, LangChain, Google ADK and OpenClaw. Pricing is usage-based and self-serve: Free ($0, 3 inboxes / 3k emails per month), Developer ($20/mo), Startup ($200/mo), Enterprise custom — explicitly no per-seat charges on API access.
profile.category: AI agent infrastructure / email API (dev tools)

profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product's end user: AgentMail sells inboxes that autonomous agents own and operate — signing up for services, receiving confirmations, authenticating, and running email threads with no human in the loop (their AISDR case study cites thousands of emails/week fully unattended). Internally, per Adi Singh's testimonial, they run Hyperspell's "company brain" as a shared source of truth across the human team and their internal agents, which they say lets them automate most internal operations, customer support especially.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Small (~10 person) dev-tools team fielding high-volume developer support across docs, Discord, email and a large SEO blog surface; support answers must be grounded in constantly-shipping product docs. They wanted one retrieval layer both humans and their internal support agents query rather than building ingestion/search themselves. Thematically aligned too — they publish content arguing email is itself agent memory and identity ("email as memory for AI agents", "the next trillion users need an identity"), so a persistent-context vendor is an adjacent, well-understood purchase rather than a leap.

profile.name: Opennote
profile.what_it_does: IMPORTANT STATUS CHANGE: Opennote was acquired by Reducto (SF document-intelligence company) and the product was SUNSET on 2026-05-06. The site now serves only a farewell notice; YC lists the company status as 'Acquired'. The embedded AI was branded 'Feynman' — per YC it 'edits your writing, references your knowledge and the web, runs background tasks, and gives feedback as you work'. Mem0's case study describes the platform as serving exploratory, self-directed learning. Scale claim on the YC page: 55,000+ students. Reducto's rationale for the acquisition: 'Their experience building products that help people work through complex, unstructured information will sharpen how we build for agents and the people using them.'
profile.category: Consumer edtech / AI tutoring (AI-native study + note-taking app). Now folded into document-intelligence infrastructure (Reducto).

profile.headcount_estimate: 3 (team size listed on the YC company directory page). All three headcount slots are the co-founders — this was a three-person company at the time of the Mem0 case study.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Summer 2025 batch (S25). Note: the S24 batch reference in the brief belongs to Mem0/Embedchain, the vendor, not to Opennote.
profile.founded_year: 2025 (per YC company directory)
profile.sells_to: Prosumer / B2C — individual students (and peer study groups). Not an enterprise or developer sale. Founders were themselves undergraduate CS/software-engineering students with tutoring and TA backgrounds, selling to their own demographic.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents were the product, not a back-office tool. 'Feynman-2' was their AI tutoring engine — an in-workspace tutor agent that explained concepts, generated interactive diagrams, edited the student's writing, referenced both the student's own notes and the web, ran background tasks, and gave feedback mid-session. Mem0 sat inside Feynman-2 to drive per-student 'learner profiles' spanning the whole platform and all its tools, so the tutor could open with things like 'You highlighted the chain rule diagram yesterday — want to apply it to this example?' or 'You stopped at Newton's Second Law. Would you like a quick recap before moving to momentum?'
profile.why_they_need_memory: Three stated drivers, all classic for this category. (1) Session fragmentation: the tutor could not recall a student's prior questions, struggles or learning path, so every session restarted cold — fatal for a tutoring product whose value proposition is continuity. (2) Token cost/latency: they were stuffing full interaction histories into prompts; Mem0 cut token usage per prompt by 40%. (3) Build-vs-buy on a 3-person team: they estimated 3-4 weeks to build memory infrastructure in-house and integrated Mem0 in 2 days with no changes to core infrastructure. This is the archetypal buyer for agent-memory: a tiny AI-native team whose product is a long-lived personalized agent, where memory is core UX but not core IP, and engineer-weeks are the scarcest resource.

Their editorial coverage is heavily agent-focused, which is the more likely reason Zep's team engaged with them.
profile.why_they_need_memory: WEAK / UNVERIFIED. A temporal knowledge graph is a genuinely natural fit for their stated 'intelligence layer' (entity resolution across papers, repos, models and people, with technique lineage tracked over time), so the category fit is plausible. But the evidence of purchase is not there. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON THE SOURCE: Zep's homepage testimonial is attributed to 'Lior Sinclair, Founder/CEO, AlphaSignal' and hyperlinks to LinkedIn activity 7287958207971434496 — which I fetched and confirmed is a Zep AI COMPANY repost of a third-party post. Cuts response time by 90%'), i.e. newsletter-style coverage, not a statement of use. profile.name: Amorphic Labs
profile.what_it_does: Agent-commerce infrastructure. Homepage tagline is "Building the software commerce infrastructure for agents" (marketing site is a one-page holding page; the actual product lives at agentmuxer.com, which 307-redirects to app.agentmuxer.com). The product, AgentMuxer, is a capability marketplace and router that lets AI agents discover, pay for, and call third-party APIs, data, and software at runtime. Per the YC profile it "routes requests to optimal providers based on real-task benchmarks and agent feedback, consolidating multiple tool accounts into a single balance and MCP connection." The live app is in Beta and advertises 2,013 publishers across 8,521 listings in 46 capability categories (finance, web search, scraping, healthcare, real estate, government data, AI services). Billing is pay-per-call, ranging from free (Firecrawl, GLEIF, Internet Archive) to ~$1.00/call (Browser Use), with most providers at $0.001-$0.75 per call; new accounts get $10 credit. Agents connect via a "buyer MCP" server. Listings carry trust tiers (Verified/Indexed) and protocol labels (HTTP). IMPORTANT NAME COLLISION: the LinkedIn page at /company/amorphiclabs is a DIFFERENT, unrelated entity (amorphiclabs.in, Chennai, India, 1 employee, consumer AI apps/games). The Glen customer is the YC S26 San Francisco company at amorphiclabs.com, confirmed by the testimonial attribution "Frank, Co-Founder & CTO" matching YC-listed CTO Frank Li.

It scraped the web daily for buying-intent signals (hiring posts, funding news, tech-stack changes, blog/press activity), sourced and verified matching leads against your ICP, researched each account, then drafted and sent personalized email and LinkedIn outreach through connected accounts. The founder described it as a "reverse Google": instead of SEO results, it surfaced actual people with the specific need your product solves, deliberately capped at 50 emails + 25 LinkedIn invites per account per day (explicitly anti-blast). Later product lines: "Associates" (AI account executives, launched Nov 2024), user-buildable agents with tools/sources (Apollo, Salesforce, HubSpot, Gmail, Outlook, web search/scrape, document extraction), natural-language automations, publishable internal/external agents, AI-native lead-capture forms, and a unified inbox where a human reviewed and approved every agent action. Pricing was usage-based at ~$1 per lead sourced/researched/contacted ($250/250 leads, $500/500 leads, custom enterprise). Claimed 1,000+ teams and named customers/case studies including Paddle, Latonas, 403 Tech, Mission Cyber Group, First Degree Capital and Stellarup. IMPORTANT STATUS: SHUT DOWN. On 30 Apr 2025 founder Mert Deveci published "Godmode: Disabled" — after ~2 years they sunset the product, closed the company and returned capital to investors despite 3+ years of runway. profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents were the entire product surface: (1) "AI Associates" — autonomous account executives that scoured the web nightly for intent signals, sourced and verified leads and drafted outreach, notifying the human each morning for approval; (2) user-built research agents wired to Apollo/Salesforce/HubSpot/Gmail/Outlook/web search/scrape/document extraction, invoked in natural language and publishable to coworkers or customers; (3) multi-step natural-language automations chaining research → summarize → draft → send; (4) an agent-configuration layer holding "full context of your business and your value propositions," formatting rules, purpose and a document knowledge base; (5) a review inbox where every proposed agent action (e.g. "Send email to Martin") required human accept-and-send.

profile.name: Mastra
profile.what_it_does: Open-source TypeScript/JavaScript framework for building AI agents and agentic applications, plus a commercial hosted cloud. Apache 2.0, ~27.7k GitHub stars, millions of monthly downloads. Core primitives: agents (LLM + tools + instructions, unified across 90+ model providers), workflows (multi-step orchestration with control flow), memory, and observability (traces, metrics, evals, datasets). Mastra Cloud sells hosting/runtime: Starter free (100K observability events then $10/100K, 24 CPU hours then $0.35/hr, 15-day retention), Teams $250/month (1M events then $8/100K, 250 CPU hours then $0.25/hr, 6-month retention, SSO, SOC 2 docs), Enterprise custom (unlimited retention, RBAC, audit logs, uptime SLAs, on-prem, dedicated support engineer, weekday SRE coverage). Ships a fast 2026 feature cadence — sandboxes with computer use, Helm charts for self-hosting, token limiting/cost control, fine-grained authorization, multi-turn evals, AI SDK v7 support. Named users on the site: Replit, Salesforce, Sanity, MongoDB, Brex.
profile.category: TypeScript agent framework + agent hosting/observability cloud (dev tools / AI infrastructure)
profile.stage: Series A
profile.funding: $35M total raised, including a $22M Series A. Investors: Spark Capital, Gradient, basecase, and Y Combinator. The YC company page corroborates 'Series A ($22M raised as of April 2026).' No valuation disclosed.
profile.headcount_estimate: ~30-35. Mastra's own /about page states 35 employees, fully remote/globally distributed with a San Francisco base; the YC profile lists team size 30. Both first-party-ish, so ~30-35 is well supported.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2025 batch (W25). Group partner: Gustaf Alstromer. YC is also listed among its investors.
profile.founded_year: 2024 (GitHub repo mastra-ai/mastra created 2024-08-06; YC profile says founded 2024)
profile.sells_to: Primarily developers (bottoms-up OSS adoption in the TypeScript/Node ecosystem), converting to B2B teams and enterprise via Mastra Cloud — a $250/mo Teams tier and an Enterprise tier with SSO/RBAC/audit logs/SLAs/on-prem.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents are the core primitive of the framework and the unit of billing in the cloud — customers define agents with tools and instructions, compose them into workflows, and deploy them onto Mastra's runtime with observability and evals attached. Mastra's three stated customer patterns are internal automation agents (e.g. Slack-based), customer-facing agents embedded in products, and developer-platform agents run as shared infrastructure. Documented customer workloads: automated customer support, CAD diagram generation, web scraping, medical transcription, financial document generation, and code-generation products.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Same pattern as CrewAI: memory is a first-party primitive, so Mastra is a substitute rather than a buyer. Mastra ships message history (on by default), working memory ('persistent, structured user data such as names, preferences, and goals' injected as system messages), semantic recall (same-thread and cross-thread), and observational memory (background agents compress older messages into 'dense observations' for long conversations), all over pluggable storage providers (LibSQL as the quickstart), with configurable memory processors for context-window pressure and per-request memory switching via RequestContext. Mastra's memory docs make no mention of Mem0 or any third-party memory vendor. Mem0's /integrations page frames the relationship as 'Use Mastra agents with Mem0 as the memory backend for cross-conversation storage and retrieval,' and Mem0 separately publishes a competitive /compare/mem0-vs-mastra page — you do not write a comparison page against your own customer. This confirms the parent's low-confidence read: integration/ecosystem listing, not a paying account. Also relevant to the buyer thesis: Mastra's real commercial wedge is hosting + observability + governance, the same 'agent control plane' territory memory vendors are expanding into.

profile.how_they_use_agents: The product IS the agent: a persistent voice-based AI tutor persona that the learner talks to daily. The site explicitly says tutors 'maintain conversation context and learning history,' give real-time corrections mid-dialogue without breaking the flow, and drive personalized study plans. The CEO frames the differentiator as tone of voice and mimicking human-to-human interaction — meaning the agent's continuity and personality, not just its answers, are the product.
profile.why_they_need_memory: A tutor that forgets is not a tutor. The agent needs to remember which words this learner keeps mispronouncing, what grammar was drilled last week, their level, goals (exam prep vs. travel vs. work), interests to keep conversation topical, and prior corrections — so it can spaced-repeat and escalate difficulty instead of restarting every session. It also needs the relationship to feel continuous, since retention in a $8/month consumer subscription depends on the avatar feeling like it knows you. That is long-running per-user episodic memory across thousands of short sessions, at millions-of-users scale where per-session cost matters — a textbook fit for a dedicated memory layer over stuffing transcripts into context.

profile.why_they_need_memory: This is the textbook agent-memory buyer. A health coach is worthless if it forgets: the coach has to hold a user's stated "why," their goals, past commitments, what they tried and abandoned, dietary constraints, injuries, and a longitudinal stream of sleep/activity/nutrition data - then reason over how all of that changed over weeks and months. Their own FAQ frames it as the coach "continuously learns from your interactions and changes its guidance to meet you where you are." Motivational interviewing in particular is a technique that depends on referencing what the person said in earlier sessions. That is exactly the temporal-knowledge-graph problem Zep/Graphiti sells: facts that are true for a period and then superseded (weight, medication, goal, job stress), plus retrieval that mixes conversation history with structured business/biometric data. Add HIPAA/SOC 2 scope and a governed, auditable memory store with provenance beats rolling their own vector-store hack.

Their multi-month task framing ("tennis lessons in my schedule for the next 6 months") implies long-horizon state that must outlive any single context window.

profile.name: Superagent
profile.what_it_does: Security layer for AI-native developers — i.e. security for teams whose code is largely written by coding agents. Five products: PR Scans (security review of pull requests before merge, catching malicious dependencies and supply-chain attacks), Contributor Trust (scoring/verifying contributor credibility), Runtime Guardrails (deterministic rules governing what an agent may do), Context Guardrails (inspecting untrusted data before an agent ingests it, i.e. prompt-injection defense), and Red Team (adversarial testing against production systems). Backed by SuperagentLM, a model they trained for agentic security that reasons about attacks rather than pattern-matching static rules. Strong open-source presence under github.com/superagent-ai: superagent (6.7k stars), grok-cli (3.5k), vibekit (1.9k), reag (904), brin ('credit score for context', 50). Note a clear pivot: Superagent began as an open-source AI agent/assistant framework and repositioned into agent security. Self-serve pricing: free (100 credits/mo), Starter $499/mo, Growth $1,499/mo, Scale from $3,999/mo; free for public open-source repos; every plan includes API and MCP access and unlimited seats. profile.name: Vela
profile.what_it_does: AI scheduling coordinator sold to professional services firms — executive search and recruiting, law, consulting, and business development teams. Vela is an agent you CC on an email (vela@yourdomain.com) or text directly; it reads the thread's context, pulls availability from your calendar and from all participants, does the timezone math, proposes real options in each person's local time, follows up with non-responders, books the meeting, sends confirmations and reminders, and re-coordinates automatically when someone needs to reschedule. Explicit design goal is zero workflow change: it works over channels people already use — email (Gmail/Outlook), SMS, WhatsApp, Slack, Teams and phone — rather than asking anyone to adopt a booking link or new app. The site includes an ROI calculator by persona (associate, lawyer, business development, partner/director) showing roughly 13 hours/month saved at 15 meetings/week, and says Vela schedules thousands of meetings each week. Sales motion is demo-only — no public pricing, no self-serve signup. Contact is a Michigan (248) phone number with an SF HQ address.

Presumably includes the standard YC deal, but no dollar figure is published — do not assume one. No Crunchbase/TechCrunch round record found.

Given a Winter 2026 batch, the true full-time count is probably in the low single digits to low teens; treat 15 as an upper bound.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2026 batch. Also Z Fellows and Pareto Holdings.
profile.founded_year: 2026 (per YC profile; company is brand new)
profile.sells_to: B2B, professional services firms — executive recruiters and search firms first, plus law firms, consultancies (LinkedIn copy references people at McKinsey and BCG) and BD teams. SMB-to-mid-market services firms rather than pure enterprise; the site name-drops end clients its customers work with (Netflix, LinkedIn, SanDisk, AWS).
profile.how_they_use_agents: Vela is a single autonomous agent that owns the whole scheduling loop with no human in it: parse intent from a natural-language email or text, identify participants, read calendar state, negotiate across parties over separate channels (one participant on email, another on WhatsApp), propose and hold slots, book, confirm, remind, and re-run the entire negotiation on a cancellation. Multi-attendee and international-timezone coordination are called out as first-class cases, as are per-user meeting-type preferences.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Scheduling is the canonical stateful agent problem, and Vela's architecture makes it acute. A single meeting negotiation spans days, multiple channels (email plus SMS plus WhatsApp) and multiple humans, so the agent must carry one coherent thread of state across sessions and mediums — no context window survives that. It also needs durable per-principal preference memory: meeting-type defaults, buffer rules, which days a partner protects, who is a VIP worth double-booking around, how a given candidate or client prefers to be contacted, and the outcome of past coordination with that same person. In executive recruiting the same candidates and hiring managers recur across searches, so remembering prior interactions is what separates it from a booking link. Rescheduling explicitly requires recalling the original negotiation. And with a two-to-fifteen person team in their first year, buying a memory layer instead of building durable cross-channel agent state is the fastest path to shipping.

profile.how_they_use_agents: The clearest large-scale agent-memory deployment of the three. Per Letta's case study: Bilt runs a memory-augmented agent architecture for personalized local-merchant and neighborhood-benefit recommendations. Architecture: unstructured transaction data is processed asynchronously in BATCH MODE with a strong model (Anthropic batch mode) to write shared Letta memory blocks; a cheaper, faster model then does real-time inference against those blocks — sophistication without frontier-model latency/cost per request. They first tried fine-tuning and rejected it ('The fine tuned model was very matter-of-fact and lost its creativity' — Kosta Krauth, CTO). Scale: over 1 million agents in production, scaling from one agent per benefit per user toward tens of millions across the user base; 'All the latency in the end-to-end system is 99+ percent just inference time' and 'Scaling from the perspective of agents is no longer a concern' (Andrew Fitz, lead engineer on the AI personalization project). Notably non-technical: PMs, team leads, GMs and the CEO all worked inside Letta's Agent Development Environment editing prompts and agent behavior. Case study first archived July 2025.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Per-user persistent state at consumer scale. Their recommendation problem is not retrieval over documents — it is remembering an individual's evolving behavior (Letta's example: recognizing timing-dependent patterns, not just static preferences) across millions of members, with an explanation attached. Fine-tuning collapsed the nuance; RAG alone doesn't hold user state. Memory blocks let them (a) separate expensive memory-writing from cheap real-time reads, (b) keep a durable per-user profile that improves without retraining, and (c) expose that state as human-editable text business staff can inspect and steer. This is the archetypal buyer for the category: a large non-AI-native consumer company with millions of users, high per-request cost sensitivity, and a personalization problem.

profile.how_they_use_agents: The 'Digital Twin' itself is the AI engine: it ingests continuous sensor and lifestyle data and generates individualized, real-time guidance ('sees how your unique biology responds to your routine'). profile.why_they_need_memory: This is the strongest memory use case of the three. A member relationship runs for years and is defined by change over time: A1c trending down, medications being titrated and discontinued, foods that spike this specific person, injuries, pregnancies, adherence patterns, what a coach told them three months ago. Any AI touching a patient must not contradict the care plan or forget a contraindication, and it must know what was true then versus what is true now — which is precisely the bi-temporal knowledge-graph proposition. Add HIPAA: Zep advertises SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA, which is likely why a regulated care company can buy a hosted memory layer at all. Multiply by a claimed 2.1M members and you need durable, retrievable, governed per-patient state rather than long prompts.

profile.name: Fleetline
profile.what_it_does: AI dispatch and load-planning software for mid-to-large trucking fleets. The engine ingests a fleet's load, driver, and ELD/TMS data and, per their own copy, "simulates billions of possible ways to plan a fleet over a week and selects the optimal one," then recommends load assignments to dispatchers. Covers both pre-booked contract freight and spot-market loads. Other surfaces: an aggregated load board pulling broker, public-board and direct-customer freight into one workspace; a "ChatGPT-like assistant trained on your fleet history and TMS data"; predictive analytics for delays, breakdowns and regulatory (HOS) violations; and network-health/profitability dashboards. Claimed outcomes: 14% revenue increase, 12% utilization increase, 52% reduction in time spent planning (og copy claims revenue growth "up to 25%"). Stated deployment path is ~65 days from ROI evaluation through TMS/ELD integration and onsite training. Legal entity "Fleetline, Inc." Note the marketing site at fleetline.ai is a Next.js shell that iframes a Framer site (fleetline.framer.website), which is why a naive fetch of the homepage returns almost nothing.

profile.name: Chroma
profile.what_it_does: Open-source (Apache 2.0) search and retrieval infrastructure for AI applications. Started as an embedding/vector database with a deliberately small 4-function API ('as easy as getting started with SQLite'); has since broadened into general search infrastructure supporting dense vector search, sparse vector search (BM25/SPLADE), full-text and trigram/regex search, and metadata filtering, over a serverless architecture built on object storage with automatic tiering between memory cache, SSD and S3/GCS. profile.name: WalkMe
profile.what_it_does: WalkMe invented and leads the Digital Adoption Platform (DAP) category. It is a no-code overlay layer that sits on top of other enterprise applications (SAP, Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Microsoft Dynamics 365, plus internal/homegrown apps) and delivers in-app guidance, walkthroughs, onboarding flows, task automation, training simulations, and adoption/usage analytics. Its differentiating tech is 'DeepUI', which reads and understands the screen of an arbitrary application so guidance can be attached to UI elements without integrating with that app's API. Customers use it to drive software adoption, cut support tickets, reduce onboarding time, enforce process compliance, and rationalize SaaS license spend. Own site claims ~1,600 customers and ~35M end users across 42+ countries. Since September 2024 it has been a wholly owned SAP company; SAP is folding DAP capabilities into its own stack alongside Joule.
profile.category: Digital adoption platform / enterprise software (SAP subsidiary) — not an agent-memory-adjacent startup; a large enterprise software buyer
profile.stage: Acquired — was VC-backed (Series A through G), IPO'd on NASDAQ June 2021, taken private by SAP September 2024. Now an SAP business unit.
profile.funding: ~$307.5M in venture funding across Series A-G (2012-2019); IPO June 16, 2021 at a ~$2.56B valuation; acquired by SAP for ~$1.5B (announced June 2024, closed September 2024, a ~45% premium to the pre-announcement share price). No independent fundraising post-acquisition.
profile.headcount_estimate: ~1,000-1,300. LinkedIn shows 1,001-5,000 with ~1,226 employees listed; Wikipedia cites 1,100; WalkMe's own About page says '900+'. Post-SAP-acquisition headcount is not separately disclosed.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None known — no accelerator affiliation; traditional Israeli/Silicon Valley VC path (Giza, Mangrove, Scale Venture Partners, Insight, Vitruvian and others across rounds).
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise. Large and very large organizations, sold primarily to IT / CIO / digital transformation offices, then extended to HR, sales ops, customer care, and public sector. Classic top-down enterprise motion with security review, procurement, and multi-year contracts.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places. (1) In the product: WalkMe now markets 'contextual AI assistance' in three modes — Pinned AI (validation embedded in a workflow step), Proactive AI (reads screen context and surfaces the next action unprompted), and On-Demand AI (conversational Q&A inside any app). It is explicitly RAG-grounded in the customer's own documentation and policies rather than a general model, and WalkMe has announced an 'agentic WalkMe experience' where admins build adoption solutions through plain-language conversation. (2) Internally — the relevant use for this research: WalkMe's own IT org used Tribal to build a customer Health Monitor that runs natively inside Salesforce. The testimonial from Tal Carmi stresses that it 'runs natively in Salesforce, meets every security standard, and never exposes our data outside our trusted environment.' So WalkMe is an internal-IT buyer of an agent-building platform, not a buyer of agent memory for its own shipped product.
profile.why_they_need_memory: The stated buying trigger is data residency and enterprise-grade context, not memory per se. WalkMe's IT wanted an agent that reasons over live Salesforce customer data (health scoring across ~1,600 accounts) without that data leaving their trusted environment. Any such agent needs durable, governed context: the Salesforce object model and metadata, what 'healthy' means for their business, prior scoring rationale, and account history over time. Their own product has the same shape of need — DeepUI plus RAG over customer policy documents is effectively an organizational memory layer for guidance. The generalizable pull is: an enterprise IT function with a mature system of record wants agents grounded in company-specific context, inside the security perimeter.

profile.name: Agentplace
profile.what_it_does: SaaS platform for building AI agents that are complete web applications rather than chat widgets. Each agent gets its own React frontend served at its own URL, a real backend that can install packages and hold business logic, a dedicated isolated VM, and a 'Brain' (model loop + tools + sub-agents + memory) with owner-selectable model. The owner describes the outcome in plain language; the builder writes the frontend/backend/integrations, tests its own work (messages the agent it built, reads replies, takes screenshots, checks logs, fixes issues), and publishes to a live URL. Two runtime modes: Site mode (the agent IS the website) and chat mode, with memory shared across both. Ships realtime voice, business records with server-enforced access classes (Catalog/Log/Per-visitor), sub-agents, web search with citations, deep research, sandboxed code execution, self-scheduling, agent-to-agent calls, GitHub push/pull, hundreds of app integrations, and an automatic MCP endpoint on every published agent (usable from Claude Code/Desktop/Cursor). Go-to-market copy targets SMB customer-facing automation: AI receptionists, booking, customer service, payments, with vertical guides for HVAC, salons, plumbing, healthcare. Pricing: Free $0 (2,000 AI credits), Pro $29/mo (15,000+ credits, 1 custom domain), Business custom (advanced security/access controls, private cloud).

Explicitly pitched to non-technical solopreneurs and small service businesses ('no code is required from the owner at any point'), with a developer-adjacent surface via GitHub sync and the auto-provisioned MCP address. profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product, not an internal efficiency tool. Agentplace sells agent infrastructure: the customer's agent is a deployed web app with its own VM, backend, and model loop. Agents appear at three layers — (1) the builder is itself an agent that writes, tests, screenshots and debugs the agent it is constructing; (2) the built agent runs a tool-calling loop with sub-agents for general work, code execution and page fetching; (3) published agents call each other agent-to-agent and expose MCP so external agents (Claude Code, Cursor) can drive them. profile.why_they_need_memory: Genuine structural need, but note they already build their own. Their llms.txt lists memory as a first-class runtime component ('Brain: the model loop, tools, sub-agents and memory'), advertises memory shared across site and chat mode, and claims the agent 'remembers people across conversations, so a visitor does not have to repeat what they already said.' They also run per-visitor business records with server-enforced access classes — effectively scoped memory with an authorization model. So they are as much a builder of agent memory as a buyer of it; a memory vendor sells to them only as a component swap, not a greenfield need. I could not locate the review — Product Hunt's 'trace-6' slug is an unrelated 2022 sneaker-consignment product (jointrace.co, 2 upvotes), and its reviews page reads 'No reviews yet.' Mariam Grigoryan does appear active in Agentplace's Product Hunt community discussions but is not among the four employees LinkedIn surfaces. profile.why_they_need_memory: Their product IS an organizational memory problem. An interview agent talking to hundreds of employees over a 1-2 week engagement has to carry context across sessions (what department X already said, which handoff was already described, which contradiction needs probing) and progressively build a single coherent org-level model rather than N disconnected transcripts. That is exactly the structured-extraction-plus-graph-retrieval shape Maximem sells: entities (people, teams, systems, handoffs) and relationships accumulated across many conversations, retrieved mid-interview. They also need an audit-grade evidence trail linking every roadmap recommendation back to the specific interview turns that produced it - a provenance requirement a raw vector store handles poorly. Secondary need: per-account persistence, so a returning client's map updates rather than restarts.

Tagline on site: "An agent to do your work & an everything app to manage it" / "One place for email, CRM, meetings, tasks, and AI." It unifies (a) native email + messaging — Gmail, Outlook, LinkedIn, Slack, iMessage, WhatsApp, X, Instagram in one inbox with AI triage, auto-labeling and drafted replies; (b) a self-updating CRM — contacts, companies, deals, auto-enrichment, "relationship warmth", network history, records that update themselves after every email and meeting; (c) meetings — calendar, notetaker, transcripts, AI prep briefs, auto-extracted action items; (d) project management — tasks, kanban, docs; (e) "custom apps" generated from a prompt (prompt-to-app with live Micro data). On top sits a Skills / Automations / Plugins marketplace (packaged bundles like "Founder Mode", "Sales", "Investor Essentials", "Product Hunt Launch") and a developer surface called Micro Blocks (TypeScript/Python/Go SDKs, REST API, CLI, MCP; advertised as working with Claude, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes). Claims 1000+ integrations. Pricing is Standard / Pro / Enterprise with a 14-day trial and a credit-metered AI allowance (6,000 and 20,000 credits/mo); Enterprise adds shared workspaces, SSO/SAML, admin controls. CASA Tier 3 certified (verified by Google). NOTE: identification is now confirmed rather than a best guess — micro.so's own homepage carries a strip reading "Built, supported and used by people at top startups, enterprises, and investment funds" whose first logo is "hyperspell" (alongside superpower, recall, mastra, valley). profile.sells_to: prosumer / B2B SMB — explicitly aimed at founders, operators, salespeople and investors ("For founders and professionals getting started"), with an Enterprise tier for teams (shared CRM, SSO/SAML, admin controls). Not a developer-first product, though it ships an API/MCP layer.
profile.how_they_use_agents: The agent IS the product, not a feature bolted on. Micro runs background automations (auto-labeling new mail and drafting replies for customers/investors/hiring; keeping people, companies, deals and tasks fresh as conversations change; turning calls into notes, decisions, owners and next steps; enriching contacts with dozens of datapoints). It surfaces proactive "Threads" — e.g. "Check back in with Corgi and Mastra on their pilot" — where it has already pulled the last replies, open tasks and the channel where the team discussed next steps. It has a command surface that does tasks on request ("Draft email to John", "Summarize unread investor emails") with human accept/reject on sensitive sends. It generates small internal apps from a prompt. And via Micro Blocks it exposes MCP/API so other agents (Claude, Codex, Cursor) can build on the workspace. It also publishes downloadable "Agentic Fundraising / Sales / Hiring / Content / Investing" skill packs for use in third-party AI tools.
profile.why_they_need_memory: This is the clearest fit of the three, and the reciprocity confirms it. Micro's entire value proposition is cross-source context: it has a dedicated homepage section titled "Micro knows you better than anyone else — Micro remembers everything from your work and conversations. It dreams and takes notes to keep everything fresh," showing memory buckets for Priorities, Work, Network, Memory, My Company, Meetings and Preferences, and a section on being "Powered by you and your team's personal context graph." To deliver that with a 2-10 person team they would otherwise have to build and maintain 1000+ OAuth connectors, permission inheritance, incremental sync, freshness, a context/entity graph across email + messages + calendar + CRM + docs, and per-user preference memory — precisely the ETL-forever problem Hyperspell's pitch targets. They are also the ideal buyer profile: AI-native, tiny team, memory is a core surface rather than a nice-to-have, and they still need it to be permission-aware for the Enterprise tier.

Features are a 24/7 AI tutor/chat, voice mode, personalized study plans, AI-generated flashcards, quizzes, mock exams/practice tests, summaries, and a homework scanner — layered on top of its original asset, a UGC library of student-authored study notes (claims 1.6M+ notes) contributed by 'Knowers' via a Creator Program. Claims 30M+ students across 30-32 countries and 170K+ app-store ratings; #1 education app in several markets. Legal entities: Knowunity GmbH (Julie-Wolfthorn Str. 1, 10115 Berlin) and Knowunity Inc. (US App Store seller). A small B2B arm sells Gen-Z employer-branding/apprenticeship recruiting to companies (e.g. a joint webinar with MAN Truck & Bus).
profile.category: Consumer edtech / AI study companion (B2C mobile app, freemium subscription), with a small B2B Gen-Z advertising & recruiting arm
profile.stage: Series B (or later) — €27M Series B announced June 2025; company now self-reports '$50m raised to date', suggesting an extension or later round beyond publicly indexed rounds
profile.funding: $50M+ total, self-reported on knowunity.com/careers and their LinkedIn 'About' ('a lean team of 60 people and $50m raised to date'). Disclosed rounds per EU-Startups headlines: €2M seed (April 2021, led by Project A Ventures), €10M (May 2022), €27M Series B (June 2025). Article bodies were Cloudflare-blocked, so investor lists beyond Project A Ventures are unconfirmed.
profile.headcount_estimate: ~55-60 core employees (careers page: 'a driven team of 55'; LinkedIn About: 'lean team of 60'). LinkedIn lists 174 associated profiles and a 51-200 size band — the gap is likely creators/interns/alumni. Hiring is Berlin-onsite (engineering, design, CEO office) plus one US remote creator role.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None found — not YC. Institutionally VC-backed; Project A Ventures led the seed.
profile.founded_year: ~2019-2020 (unconfirmed exact). knowunity.de was first archived Nov 2019 and the iOS app id (1484296272) dates to late 2019; the seed round in April 2021 described the company as Stuttgart-based, before the move to Berlin.
profile.sells_to: B2C / prosumer — students (freemium subscription, parents pay). Secondary B2B SMB-to-enterprise motion selling Gen-Z employer branding and apprenticeship recruiting.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Three distinct surfaces. (1) In product: Knowie, a conversational AI tutor with voice mode, generating flashcards, quizzes, mock exams and study plans from the user's actual curriculum; they report crossing 2T+ tokens processed in a year, self-describing as 'one of Europe's largest AI providers.' (2) Internally, they are aggressively agent-operated: background/remote agents pick up shake-to-report bug reports from the app, fix them, and open reviewed PRs; design reviews are automated with feedback posted to Slack in minutes; marketing built an agent tool that analyzes social hooks and generates creative across 30 countries. (3) With cognee: VP & co-founder Gregor Weber's team built a Neo4j knowledge graph over metadata for 40,000 students in Bremen (grade level, school type, anonymized IP-address patterns) modeled as five entities (User, Grade, SchoolType, IPAddress, Connection), with weighted shared-IP edges, densest-subgraph detection and academic-similarity matching, queryable both in Cypher and in natural language — to recommend study groups and peer connections. POC delivered in 2 days, GDPR-compliant. NOTE on is_ai_native=false: founded ~2019 as a UGC note-sharing app and pivoted to AI; today it is emphatically AI-first ('AI native across the org'), so treat the flag as 'not AI-native by founding date' rather than 'not an AI company.'
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two reasons, and the stated one is the more interesting. Explicitly: relational reasoning over their user base broke both existing approaches — 'SQLs got out of hand and embeddings were too sparse' for questions about proximity and relationship between students. A graph memory layer was the only representation that handled multi-hop social/academic structure (same school, same neighborhood, same struggle). Implicitly: their entire product thesis is a companion 'that knows you, adapts to you and guides you every day' across a multi-year school career — which is a long-horizon per-user memory problem, not a context-window problem. They bought cognee for the first (a relationship graph) but the second is the durable pull.

profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents are a 2026 product layer on top of a 2020-founded payments platform, announced Jul 30 2026 as 'intelligence in every layer of embedded payments'. (1) Amigo AI agent suite — Amigo Insights is live: natural-language querying of live payment data (funding status, chargebacks, residuals, merchant demographics) replacing manual reporting; roadmap includes Amigo Risk (proactive transaction monitoring), Amigo Chargebacks (auto-gathers evidence and drafts dispute responses), Amigo Boarding (walks merchants through onboarding), Amigo Underwriting (risk assessment to cut manual review), Amigo Pricing & Billing (rate optimization, fee calc, residuals). profile.why_they_need_memory: ~125 people and ~50 engineers, fully remote, tripled since 2023 with a documentation function of essentially one person (Casey Smith, Director of Documentation). Confluence was the sanctioned wiki but nobody used it — knowledge lived in Google Drive and Slack threads, written once to satisfy a compliance or review requirement and then never updated. In a regulated payfac, stale internal knowledge is a compliance and risk-review problem, not just an annoyance. Two compounding drivers: (a) senior engineers were the human search index and were being interrupted constantly; (b) they are now shipping customer-facing agents and an MCP/agent-skills surface, which means their own payment operations and API semantics have to be written down accurately somewhere an agent can read. Casey Smith's framing — 'we're starting to develop a culture of writing and looking things up before asking someone; that's very important for scale' — is the buying trigger: scale-stage headcount growth outrunning tribal knowledge.

profile.how_they_use_agents: Both directions, and this is the key detail. (1) INTERNALLY / IN-PRODUCT: Middesk shipped an "Agent in the Loop" model — specialized research agents that do OFAC false-positive resolution, address-discrepancy investigation, beneficial-ownership tracing across complex structures, litigation research, continuous merchant-risk assessment, and operating-status confirmation across SOS/web-presence/activity signals. Marketing line: "Specialized agents. Structured findings with full evidence. Zero manual review queues." Reported internal results: manual review time dropped from 15-20 minutes to under 10, auto-approval rates "trending toward 50%+". They are explicit that the agent gathers evidence and the human analyst still decides. (2) OUTWARD: they publish an MCP server plus GraphQL API so third-party AI agents (they name Claude and Cursor) can verify businesses and query identity data autonomously — a product release literally titled "Infrastructure for the agentic economy". So Middesk is simultaneously an agent operator and a tool vendor to other people's agents.
profile.why_they_need_memory: The Falconer testimonial is from Dan Hanson, Product Manager, and states the pain directly: "Falconer prevents our documentation from drifting out of sync with our codebase as engineers ship new products and features. The result is like giving every team member a senior engineer they can ask questions anytime they need help understanding our product." Structural drivers: a ~140-person company with 600+ customers and a broad, fast-moving surface area (verification, fraud, underwriting, registration, liens, international); an API-first product where docs accuracy is effectively compliance-adjacent for regulated buyers; and — most relevant to the agent-memory category — they publish an MCP server, meaning their documentation is now consumed by external agents, not just humans, so doc drift becomes an agent-correctness problem. Note their own agent blog explicitly does NOT discuss internal knowledge/context management, so the Falconer use case appears to be internal engineering/product documentation rather than powering their customer-facing agents.

profile.how_they_use_agents: IMPORTANT DISCREPANCY: the brief I was given cites a Jan 15, 2026 case study 'Zurich Insurance Group Scales Underwriting Operations' with a quote from Penny Seach, Group Chief Underwriting Officer, and metrics of 42% faster case triage / 3x workflow updates / 100% traceable decision steps. None of that appears on interloom.com as of this check — there is no /case-studies path (404), no Penny Seach quote, and no such metrics. What IS live: the interloom.com homepage carries a Zurich Insurance Group logo and a testimonial from ANTONY ELLIOTT, Head of Digital R&D, saying Zurich 'saw during the Hyperchallenge great potential in how Interloom's novel approach can enable AI agents to take better decisions based on distributed and unstructured knowledge' and that they have been 'working with them on multiple use cases since we selected them as a winner.' So the verifiable relationship is an innovation-challenge win plus multiple ongoing use cases sponsored by a Digital R&D function — a pilot/evaluation footing, not a proven production underwriting deployment. Where agents would sit, per Interloom's insurance solution template: an intake agent classifies loss type, extracts fields and requests missing evidence; an integration pulls coverage limits, endorsements and prior claim history from the policy system; a senior adjuster reviews fraud signals and complex liability. Zurich itself markets no AI-agent product — agents are an internal operations technology for it.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Claims and underwriting are precedent-driven judgment work: submissions arrive across email, portals and phone as incomplete packages, teams chase documents, re-read policy language, and re-decide the same edge cases repeatedly. The expert knowledge of how a water-damage or subrogation case should be handled lives in adjusters' and underwriters' heads and in unstructured documents, not in the policy admin system — which is exactly the 'distributed and unstructured knowledge' problem Zurich's own testimonial names. Add heavy regulatory pressure (auditable decision trails, sign-off provenance) and a workforce of ~55k across 200+ territories where local practice diverges, and a durable, queryable memory of how decisions were actually made becomes the gating requirement before any agent is allowed near a case.

profile.what_it_does: Open-source AI research lab and product company. Two main lines: (1) the Hermes family of open-weight, "human-aligned" general-purpose LLMs (Hermes 4 is current), plus distributed-training research (DisTrO, Psyche) for coordinating decentralized model training; (2) Hermes Agent, an open-source, self-improving agent harness that is now its flagship product. Hermes Agent runs from a CLI or as a gateway across Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal and email, executes in sandboxes (Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Vercel Sandbox), delegates to parallel subagents, schedules work via built-in cron, and reaches 300+ models through Nous Portal. Other surfaces: Nous Chat, Nous Portal (inference API/router), and sims.nousresearch.com. Self-describes as "a frontier open source AI company" and "a leader in the American open source AI movement," fully remote with an NYC office; LinkedIn lists HQ as Austin, TX. Commercially it sells a hosted Hermes Cloud on Free/Plus/Super/Ultra tiers (roughly $20–$200/month per TechCrunch).
profile.category: AI research lab + open-source agent harness / consumer-and-developer AI agent (frontier AI lab adjacent)

profile.headcount_estimate: 11-50 (LinkedIn company page). Careers page lists ~10 open roles (Forward Deployed Engineer, ML Engineer Evals, Product Analytics, Security, several Software Engineer roles incl. Hermes Cloud and Mobile, UI/UX, NYC Office Manager), so headcount is likely growing past 50.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; began as an open-source/Discord research collective in 2023 and was funded directly by crypto-adjacent and open-source VCs (Paradigm, Robot Ventures, Delphi, OSS Capital).
profile.sells_to: Developers primarily, plus prosumer — open-source agent harness (MIT-licensed) with a paid hosted cloud tier at $20–$200/month, and open-weight models consumed by the broader AI developer community. Not an enterprise-seat B2B motion.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product. Hermes Agent is an autonomous agent harness with an explicit closed learning loop: it creates skills from experience and improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations (FTS5 full-text search with LLM summarization for cross-session recall), and "builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions." It runs long-lived across chat platforms with a unified context, spawns parallel subagents, and executes in isolated sandboxes. The GitHub README explicitly names Honcho for dialectic user modeling — i.e., Honcho is wired in as a memory/user-model backend so the agent can understand user patterns over time. Honcho's own homepage advertises this back: "Hermes Agent — Autonomous agent with built-in Honcho memory."
profile.why_they_need_memory: Structurally the most memory-dependent buyer profile in this category. Hermes Agent's core differentiation is persistence — same agent, same user, across Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/CLI, over months. That requires cross-surface identity, a durable user model, and cross-session recall that a context window cannot provide, so a user-modeling layer is a first-class dependency rather than a nice-to-have. Note the relationship is as much partnership/integration as pure purchase: Nous ships Honcho as a bundled memory backend inside an MIT-licensed open-source product, which is distribution for Honcho and a build-vs-buy shortcut for Nous. That mutual interest should be discounted when reading it as a customer proof point — though it is still the strongest-evidenced name on the list, corroborated in three independent places (Honcho homepage integration copy, Honcho's blog, and the Hermes Agent README itself).

profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product. Voice agents conduct autonomous patient phone calls at scale, backed by a proprietary "constellation architecture" — Polaris, a suite of ~22 LLMs (reported 4.2T parameters in v3.0, 5.0T+ in later versions) with specialized safety/support models supervising a primary conversational model. Integrated with 50+ EMR systems including Epic. 0.5-1% of live calls sampled for safety monitoring; agents validated across 775,000+ test calls with 7,700+ licensed U.S. clinicians. The Aug 2026 "Orchestrators" release moves from single-task agents to multi-agent workflows chasing clinical outcomes.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Strongest and most legible need of the three. Their agents hold repeated longitudinal relationships with the same patient — a chronic-care or medication-adherence agent calls the same person weekly for months. Without persistent user-level memory the agent re-asks answered questions, loses stated preferences (best time to call, language, caregiver present, prior side effects, why the patient skipped a dose), and breaks the trust the whole clinical-safety pitch depends on. EMR data covers clinical facts but not conversational/relational context. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: PHI under HIPAA makes a third-party memory vendor a hard procurement path, and their proprietary-model, in-house posture suggests they build this internally — which makes the Honcho logo more likely a developer/experiment than a production contract.

profile.how_they_use_agents: The assistant IS the product. Rokid Glasses ship a voice-first AI assistant on YodaOS doing real-time translation, audio transcription, hands-free photo/video capture and teleprompter; the Style/Neo models route to third-party LLMs (ChatGPT and Gemini) rather than a purely in-house model. EverMind's own framing for the (unshipped) integration is 'long-term memory for all of your smart activities'. Concretely: remembering people, places, prior conversations and standing preferences across sessions and devices; making transcription/translation history retrievable later; and personalising a voice-only interface where there is no screen to re-enter context on. Rokid is also multi-LLM (ChatGPT + Gemini), which pushes memory out of any one model provider and into a portable layer — exactly the pitch of a 'company brain' vendor.

(1) In the product: 'Dottie' began in April 2023 as a ChatGPT-powered eQMS assistant and reached Dottie AI 5.0 in April 2026, which explicitly introduces agentic AI personas treated as 'digital employees' — a Research Agent that investigates across internal records and external sources, a Review Agent that flags gaps and compliance issues before they become bottlenecks, and a Document-to-Protocol agent that converts approved docs into structured protocol content. Governance is first-class: expert-in-the-loop approvals, configurable agent boundaries aligned to SOPs, and human coaching by authorized quality managers. (2) As a Tribal customer: CEO Doron Sitbon reports Tribal built a custom sales-compensation app (commissions, SPIFFs, bonuses) natively inside Salesforce in days, with Tribal's blog citing 60%+ faster delivery cycles, 40+ technical users shipping daily, 3 stalled projects unblocked, and 5x faster than traditional development at ~10% of the effort. profile.why_they_need_memory: Strongest and most explicit memory story of the three, and it comes from their own product marketing rather than my inference. Dottie is described as maintaining 'context-aware, long-running quality dialogues' that users can pause and resume later without losing context, with 'defensible data grounding' tethering every output to source documents so it survives an audit. In regulated life sciences, an agent's recollection is a compliance artifact: a CAPA investigation or protocol review unfolds over weeks, must cite its evidence, and must be explainable to an FDA inspector years later. That is durable, attributable, auditable agent memory — not a convenience feature. Their internal Tribal usage points the same direction: they want business users building on top of accumulated org context (comp plans, approval chains, payroll rules) without re-specifying it each time.

A semantic/context layer lets each customer's own sales ops team ask natural-language questions of their own deal data, approval bottlenecks and pricing trends without DealHub hand-building a dashboard per tenant and without handing out raw DB access — a multi-tenant governance problem as much as an analytics one. Second, their own agent strategy depends on persistent business context: the conversational quoting and pricing agents can only be 'governed' if company pricing policy, approval rules and discount guardrails live in a durable, queryable context layer rather than being re-derived per prompt. Inkle's product uses AI as feature-level assistance inside a human-in-the-loop service: AI-suggested transaction categorization, AI-enabled receipt matching, 'Smart Reconcile' AI matching for Stripe, and a mentioned 'LLM integration.' Licensed human CPAs still do the actual tax work, and their own case-study pages contain no mention of AI agents at all. There is no evidence Inkle runs an autonomous agent fleet or builds agentic products. Their appearance in this dataset is as a CUSTOMER of Poth Labs — an AI customer-intelligence tool that finds gaps in a company's customer evidence and runs adaptive AI surveys to fill them, storing responses back against customer accounts. The plausible pull is customer-account knowledge accumulation: Inkle serves 500+ small startups over multi-year compliance relationships where entity structure, filing history, jurisdictions and founder residency status must persist and compound — and Poth Labs' pitch is precisely an evolving per-account knowledge base assembled from evidence plus survey responses. But this is a GTM/customer-research use case, not core-product agent memory. Note also the citation quality: this is a logo-wall placement only — no quote, no case study, not listed as an integration — so it is unverified whether Inkle is a paying customer, a design partner, or a friendly logo (both are early-stage companies and Composio, another Poth logo, is also India-linked, suggesting a shared network rather than an enterprise sales motion).

profile.name: UnCircuit
profile.what_it_does: Custom game-based candidate assessments for hiring. A company gives UnCircuit a role brief naming the traits it cares about (judgment, creativity, pace, attention to detail, collaboration, work under pressure); UnCircuit designs a bespoke 10-30 minute scenario game around those traits; every candidate for that role plays the same short challenge (marketed as ~6 focused minutes per candidate). The platform measures behavior live - score, pace, trade-offs, 'integrity signals', how they recover when rules change mid-task - and produces an evidence report / 'clean evidence summary' the hiring team can share. Pitch is 'beyond the resume' and 'save 50+ hours on screening calls'. Go-to-market is founder-led: 'Book 14 minutes with a founder' via a cal.com link to the CEO, plus a phone number in the header. Product copy describes human-designed games plus real-time behavioral measurement ('We build a short scenario', 'We watch how they think', 'Score, pace, trade-offs, and integrity signals as they happen'). profile.why_they_need_memory: They are a Poth Labs customer, and Poth sells a persistent, citation-backed customer-knowledge layer rather than an agent-memory SDK - so the fit is operational, not in-product. UnCircuit's entire sales motion is bespoke: every deal starts as a long founder-led call where a hiring manager describes an 'ideal hire' and the traits that matter, and each game is then custom-built from that brief. That knowledge lives in call recordings, role briefs and per-customer report feedback, scattered and re-discovered each time. A persistent customer-evidence map lets a two-person team answer 'which traits do customers keep asking for', 'why did this deal stall', and 'what did this hiring team actually say' without re-interviewing. This is the clearest example in this set of a NON-agent-native buyer of the category.

profile.name: Thüga Aktiengesellschaft
profile.what_it_does: Thüga AG is a Munich-based holding and services company that is the hub of Germany's largest municipal energy network ("kommunaler Verbund"). It takes minority stakes in roughly 100 municipal utilities (Stadtwerke) and regional energy/water suppliers that together serve about 9 million people with electricity, gas, heat and water. Thüga itself does not primarily sell energy to end customers; it sells shareholding capital plus a shared-services layer to its partner utilities: strategy consulting, energy trading and procurement (pooled tender volumes), renewables project development (wind/solar), billing and meter-data process management, regulatory/insurance solutions, and IT & digitalization. It runs six specialized 'Plusgesellschaften' subsidiaries for this, including Thüga SmartService (IT, digital transformation, billing/meter-to-cash BPO) and a sales platform called PACE that the company describes as combining technology, artificial intelligence and specialized services. Founded 1867 in Gotha as Thüringer Gasgesellschaft. Not publicly traded: held via Thüga Holding GmbH & Co. KGaA, owned by Mainova AG (~20.5%), N-ERGIE (~20.5%), enercity (~20.5%) and Kom9 GmbH & Co. KG, a consortium of 53 municipal utilities (~38.4%).
profile.category: energy utility holding / municipal utility network (buyer of back-office AI, not an AI vendor)
profile.stage: Established privately held corporate (municipally owned, not venture-backed). ~159 years old.
profile.funding: Not venture-funded. Municipally owned via Thüga Holding GmbH & Co. KGaA; revenue €5.83bn (2024). No Crunchbase/PitchBook-style funding rounds exist for this entity.

profile.how_they_use_agents: UNVERIFIED AT SOURCE. Interloom's claimed case study ('Thüga Streamlines Operations Across Regional Energy Subsidiaries', Nov 15 2025; 48% less time on routine case handling, 2 subsidiaries live, 6-week deployment) could NOT be found anywhere on interloom.com as of Sept 2026 — no case study page, no logo, no mention. Interloom's own press page names only Zurich Insurance, Fiege and Volkswagen Group Services as customers, and no 'thuega' tenant subdomain appears in the Wayback archive of interloom.com (unlike vomberg, comdirect, commerzbank, adecco, jll, lenze, ruinart, vwgs, leipzigerstadtwerke and others, which all have archived single-tenant stacks). What IS verifiable from Thüga's own site: a digitalization agenda run through Thüga SmartService, a data strategy/governance program, and a sales platform called PACE described as using artificial intelligence. If the Interloom deployment is real, the shape implied is back-office case handling (billing disputes, meter faults, outage/customer cases) orchestrated across subsidiary utilities — which matches Interloom's own 'Energy: Billing & Outage Cases' solution page describing intake agents, billing/SCADA integrations and field-coordinator escalation. Treat the Thüga reference as unconfirmed.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Structurally, Thüga is close to the archetypal buyer for a 'company brain': it must deliver consistent process quality across ~100 legally independent municipal utilities that each run their own CRM, billing and dispatch stack, without being able to force them onto one shared system (exactly the tension in the quoted testimonial). Process knowledge lives in the heads of long-tenured staff at each Stadtwerk, the workforce is ageing, and the same edge cases (tariff adjustments, meter faults, regulatory changes, grid-connection requests) get re-decided independently in dozens of places. A precedent/memory layer that captures how a case was resolved at one subsidiary and makes it reusable at the next is the only way to get shared process quality without a shared ERP. Regulated environment also means decisions need an audit trail, which favors a memory system that cites its precedent.

profile.name: AI Data Technician
profile.what_it_does: NOT A COMPANY — an individual academic project by Yuan Sui, whose GitHub bio reads 'PhD @ Caltech'. AI Data Technician is an agentic system for scientists working with high-dimensional, high-sample-rate time series (multi-channel neural recordings at 1-2 kHz, wearable sensor streams, industrial vibration data). It converts raw signals into intermediate representations LLMs can reason over (spectrograms, PSD plots, statistical features), then uses interactive human-AI collaboration to formalize expert judgment into interpretable detection rules for artifact rejection, event marking and signal classification. Architecture: three agents — Orchestrator (Claude Sonnet with a 4,000-token extended-thinking budget, up to 25 tool-use iterations), Task agent (autonomous multi-step execution with bash/read/write/vision, 15 iterations), and Think agent (memory extraction, context compaction, session reflection). Tools include bash, read (PDF + MATLAB .mat v4-v7.3), write, vision (Gemini Flash), plot (Plotly + matplotlib), recall, remember, task, ask and todo, over a pre-installed scientific stack (NumPy, SciPy, MNE, antropy, ruptures, h5py, scikit-learn). Real-time WebSocket browser UI with streaming chat, live activity panel, interactive plots and a todo tracker. GitHub: 6 stars, 2 forks, repo created 2026-03-15, last push 2026-03-19, sole contributor. Demo at yue-crew-projects.org is gated behind Cloudflare Access (approval required). profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product: a three-agent loop where the Orchestrator plans with extended thinking and delegates, the Task agent autonomously executes multi-step analysis (loading files, computing features, generating and testing code), and the Think agent manages knowledge. Agents call vision models on generated plots to describe and compare signal images, and pause to ask the scientist clarifying questions via a browser modal when genuinely blocked.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Deep, well-specified dependency — arguably the most sophisticated memory design of the three. Three-layer architecture: Session (per-conversation turn/tool logs, plus raw chat turns pushed to EverMemOS via store_chat_turn() for passive fact extraction), Project (project_memory.md rewritten by the Think agent every 5 messages and injected into the system prompt each turn; in EverMemOS stored under a project-scoped group_id hashed from the project path, classified as episodic_memory vs profile and keyword-indexed for semantic retrieval), and Global (cross-project procedures and user preferences under group_id 'adt_global', populated by end-of-session reflection). The 'remember' tool writes to file and EverMemOS simultaneously in hybrid mode; 'recall' does keyword + semantic search across project and global layers then synthesizes via the Think agent. Deployment is either self-hosted Docker (ghcr.io/.../evermemos:latest) or the managed cloud service at api.evermind.ai. The stated rationale: no universal thresholds exist in signal analysis, so learned parameters, artifact signatures and labeling procedures must persist and compound across sessions.

(a) Internal/agentic — this is what Jedify is for: CTO Matthew Drooker's testimonial describes "enterprise AI agents" plus human analysts querying business data, and explicitly says agents "can't reason accurately from stitched-together connectors and warehouses alone," i.e. LLM agents over the company's own warehouse/CRM/ad/telemetry estate for analytics and agentic workflows. (b) In-product AI — mostly non-agentic ML/automation: the Max Engage "decision engine" that auto-evaluates and re-sequences broadcast content, AI-driven ad targeting signals, an Nvidia partnership for AI forecasting (2024), and AI-generated "smart NOTAMs" for pilots (Sept 2025). Their own marketing language is "augmented intelligence," and their AI pages make no mention of LLMs or agentic workflows — the agent story lives on the internal data side, not the product side.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Enormous, heterogeneous data estate accumulated over 40+ years and three owners: consumer app telemetry at hundreds of millions of users, ad-tech data, aviation/enterprise contracts, forecast model output, plus whatever schema sprawl survived the IBM-to-Francisco-Partners carve-out. The CTO's stated pain is precisely the agent-memory pitch: connectors + warehouse tables carry no business meaning, so agents hallucinate or produce answers analysts can't trust. They need a persistent, governed semantic/context layer so agents and humans resolve the same metric the same way "at Weather Company scale."

profile.how_they_use_agents: Jedify is used for internal AI-powered BI: Rory O'Flynn (Director, Insights & Analytics) says traditional self-serve BI "never reached the level we needed," and Dominic Pyne (Director, Analytics Engineering) says "anyone can answer a business question without relying on data analyst expertise or navigating dashboards" — natural-language agents over the analytics stack, replacing dashboard navigation, with an explicit buy-over-build decision. Their stated pain is the analyst bottleneck and dashboard sprawl: business users can't self-serve, and an LLM pointed at raw warehouse tables at that cardinality won't pick the right metric definition. A persistent context/semantic layer is what lets a non-technical PM or label-relations person ask a question and get an answer that matches what the analytics team would have produced — and their quote about choosing Jedify "over building in-house" shows they scoped the internal-context-layer build and decided to buy it.

profile.name: Mission Inbox
profile.what_it_does: Mission Inbox is dedicated email sending infrastructure focused on deliverability and inbox placement for high-volume senders. Rather than replacing a CRM or sequencer, it sits underneath them as the sending layer. Its differentiators: 'Isolated Cubes,' separate sending environments so sales, marketing, and transactional traffic cannot damage each other's reputation; dedicated IPs instead of shared pools; MI Shield, an AI-powered pre-send check on content, headers, DNS, and spam signals; and API, SMTP, and IMAP access plus webhooks, logs, and delivery analytics. Published pricing is transparent and low: Lite $50/mo (15 mailboxes, 5,000 sends), Scale $199/mo (30 mailboxes, 10,000 sends), Pro $99/mo for developers (5 domains, 100K sends), with $2 per extra domain and $1 per additional 1,000 sends. Marketing claims 50M+ emails processed monthly, a 98% inbox rate, and 8 redundancy layers across 3 continents. It positions explicitly against SendGrid, Mailgun, Resend, Gmail/Outlook, Mailforge, MailReef, Maildoso, and Hypertide, and integrates with HubSpot, Salesforce, Apollo, Instantly, Smartlead, Salesloft, Outreach, EmailBison, and PlusVibe. Named logos and case studies: Unit21, BloomTech, Practical Prospecting, Relay, AmpleMarket, Stream. Per LinkedIn the company rebranded and acquired CeyMail to move into transactional email, framing itself as 'mission control for every email your business sends.' Developer docs cover Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Ruby. Note the site's own framing of the deliverability problem: '52% of business emails go unseen.'
profile.category: email infrastructure / deliverability (dev tools and GTM infrastructure)
profile.stage: unknown — most likely seed-stage or bootstrapped. No funding announcement, investor, or round found in any accessible source.
profile.funding: unknown — no disclosed rounds found. Crunchbase (403) and Tracxn (404) were inaccessible and the web search budget was exhausted, so absence of evidence here is soft. The company did fund at least one acquisition (CeyMail), terms undisclosed.

profile.yc_or_accelerator: none found
profile.founded_year: 2024 (per LinkedIn)
profile.sells_to: B2B SMB and developers primarily — outbound sales teams, lead-gen agencies, recruiters, and RevOps, plus developers embedding transactional and programmatic email. Some enterprise reach (Unit21 is a named enterprise case study, where the use case was isolating cold outbound off the primary corporate domain).
profile.how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places, and the product-side one is the notable one. First, AI agents are an explicitly targeted customer segment: missioninbox.com/ai-agents is a dedicated product page offering 'email infrastructure for AI agents,' giving an agent a dedicated inbox it 'owns and operates on its own' via REST API, SMTP, IMAP, or SDKs — no human Gmail account required — plus inbound routing to the right agent or workflow, attachment handling into processing pipelines, reply threading to preserve conversation context, and webhooks that trigger agent actions on arrival, reply, or bounce. The page enumerates six agent archetypes it sells to: browser agents receiving OTPs and verification codes for automated signup, AI SDR agents doing outbound at scale, AI support agents, operations agents sending bookings/invoices/reminders, document-processing agents parsing inbound invoices and forms, and marketplace agents managing isolated inboxes per counterparty. Second, internally in the product, MI Shield is described as an AI-powered pre-send classifier that blocks risky messages before they are delivered. So Mission Inbox is picks-and-shovels for the agent economy rather than an agent company itself.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Strong fit, better than the other two. Deliverability is a domain where the value is almost entirely undocumented operational knowledge: IP warmup schedules, per-ESP quirks (what Google tolerates that Outlook does not), DNS/SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure patterns, which content signals trip filters, and per-client sending configurations. A ~13-person team supporting agencies that each run 20+ client campaigns cannot scale that by memory — Practical Prospecting alone migrated 20+ client campaigns off three other platforms in a day. The team also publishes heavy SEO content (23+ blog posts, 9 comparison pages, 9 integration pages, industry pages) largely under a single author, plus a growing docs surface in six languages, which is a content operation that benefits from a shared knowledge base. And as a company selling infrastructure to agent builders, it is culturally predisposed to adopt agent tooling in its own stack. CAVEAT ON THE VENDOR LINK: the Agently attribution is better than AppSumo's — the launch post reportedly tags @agently_ai, suggesting mutual acknowledgment — but I could not reproduce it. When I loaded agently.dev/live it showed only a rolling 4-item window of recent joins (Yarrow Field, Roamwell, Sagelight Health, Petrel & Co) with no Mission Inbox entry, and those names plus the 'shipped to X' entries look like generated placeholders. So the company is real and a plausible buyer; the confirmed purchase is not.

Important scope caveat: Cognee frames this as a 'low-risk discovery' pilot run on sample documents, not a production rollout, with expansion to co-branded and small-business portfolios described as future work.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Card product knowledge is fragmented across terms-and-conditions documents, disclosures, and branch-specific variants, so plain retrieval returned uncertain answers. Cognee's pitch was clause-level chunking (APR rules, eligibility criteria as discrete entities), a knowledge graph plus vector hybrid grounded in FIBO (Financial Industry Business Ontology), and provenance threading that links every answer back to the source clause. The buying driver is regulatory: in a regulated bank an agent answer is only usable if it is auditable, so 'memory with provenance' is the compliance unlock, not merely a quality improvement. This is the archetypal regulated-enterprise buyer for the category - high document fragmentation, low tolerance for ungrounded output, and a need to show a regulator where an answer came from.

profile.what_it_does: The company as Interloom describes it - "a precision engineering firm that manufactures complex assemblies for industrial clients" - could not be confirmed to exist. What I did find, and the reason this is flagged rather than dismissed outright: (1) RM COMPONENTS GMBH, Schwabach, Germany (O'Brien-Str. 5, 91126 Schwabach; Amtsgericht Nürnberg HRB 13887; registered 2002; LEI 529900FBHRUB0WESY754) is real and active - but it is an ELECTRONICS DISTRIBUTOR, not a manufacturer. Founded 1996 as a contract distributor for Taiyo Yuden, it distributes passive and active components (ceramic chip capacitors, inductors, ferrites, EMI suppression, diodes, MOSFETs, LDOs, quartz) from Taiyo Yuden, Holy Stone/Formosa, CapXon and Tai-Tech, and runs what it calls Europe's largest warehouse for its key suppliers. LinkedIn lists it as 11-50 employees, industry Semiconductors; its own team page shows roughly 50+ people across sales, technical support, order handling, logistics, QM, IT and finance. It has no in-house manufacturing or engineering and mentions no AI anywhere. (2) rmcomponents.com is a US steel-industry sales-representation firm on a template site with placeholder addresses ("251 Purple Sunset Bogota") - almost certainly not it. (3) UK Companies House has only two dissolved entities (R M COMPONENTS LTD 08219560, dissolved 2014; RMR PRECISION COMPONENTS LIMITED 07192317, dissolved 2014). NOTE THE PARTIAL FIT: the German distributor does do BOM processing - its 2026 webshop launch added customer BOM upload - and a distributor's inside-sales/FAE team matching customer bills of materials to catalogue parts is a genuinely good match for the claimed metrics (61% faster BOM processing, 90% field-extraction accuracy). So it is possible the vendor garbled a real customer's description. But "manufactures complex assemblies" flatly contradicts a distributor, no link is documented anywhere, and the case study itself cannot be found.

Colrows' pitch is that the reasoning must be point-in-time reproducible because an investment committee and a regulator will both ask how the number was reached — the anonymous quote used is 'The investment committee didn't ask us to justify the number. For the first time, the number came with its own justification - traceable to regulation, to precedent, to the account itself.' Their prior state — four expert disciplines working apart, with knowledge locked in individual analysts — is exactly the institutional-memory gap this category sells against.
