profile.name: AppSumo
profile.what_it_does: AppSumo is a curated deals marketplace for business software, aimed at entrepreneurs and small businesses. Software vendors list limited-time offers — most famously lifetime-access licenses — at discounts the site advertises up to 95% off, and AppSumo takes roughly half of each sale. Its own about page claims 1.5M+ entrepreneurs, $550M in cumulative customer savings, and $113M paid out to partners and affiliates; the storefront claims over 2 million customers. It runs seasonal sale events ("Sumo Day"), an affiliate program, and an "AppSumo Select" tier for vendors. Legally registered as Sumo Group, Inc. AppSumo is a distributor of AI tools rather than an AI company: its current storefront is full of third-party AI listings (PlugThis AI, FeedBoss, AIWriteBook, RobinReach, Friday Code, AahSheet), but the marketplace itself is a curation-and-commerce business. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON THE VENDOR LINK: the evidence that AppSumo buys agent memory is weak. The only citation is an auto-generated 'New companies on Agently' post for a lowercase, self-entered workspace named "appsumo," and when I loaded agently.dev/live in a browser the feed was a rolling 4-item window showing joins from Yarrow Field, Roamwell, Sagelight Health, and Petrel & Co, with 'shipped to X' posts from Argonaut Bio, Ovenbird, and Harborlight CX — a set of whimsical two-word names with identically structured one-line value props that read as generated placeholders, alongside agent activity anonymized to pseudonyms like 'Company #6420.' Anyone can type 'appsumo' into a signup field. Treat AppSumo as real (it obviously is) but not as a confirmed agent-memory customer.

profile.how_they_use_agents: No public evidence of AI agents inside AppSumo's own operations. Its relationship to AI is as a channel: it curates and merchandises other companies' AI products to its entrepreneur audience. If the Agently workspace is genuine, the plausible internal use is ops-side — a small merchandising and partner team running recurring deal vetting, vendor onboarding, support, and content workflows across tools like HubSpot, Gmail, and Notion, which is the surface Agently's connectors target. profile.why_they_need_memory: The credible pull is operational rather than product-side. AppSumo's core loop is repetitive and precedent-heavy: evaluating inbound vendor applications against the same quality and refund-risk criteria, negotiating comparable deal terms, onboarding each new partner through the same launch checklist, and fielding support on a 60-day guarantee across thousands of SKUs. That institutional knowledge — why a past deal was rejected, what terms a category normally gets, which vendors caused refund spikes — is exactly what a company-brain product claims to hold. Weighing against it: this is a 16-year-old bootstrapped commerce company with established internal systems, not a greenfield AI-native buyer, so it is not the archetypal customer for this category.

Verified infobox facts: founded 2000-01-18 by Robin Li and Eric Xu, HQ in Haidian District, Beijing; 35,900 employees as of 2024; CN¥133.1 billion revenue in 2024; listed on NASDAQ (BIDU) and HKEX (9888). Product portfolio spans Baidu Search, the Baidu App (search plus news feed), Baidu Baike (encyclopedia), Baidu Tieba (forums), Baidu Maps, and the iQIYI streaming platform. Beyond consumer internet, Baidu operates a full-stack AI business: Baidu AI Cloud, in-house AI accelerator silicon (Kunlun), foundation models, and the Apollo autonomous-driving program including the Apollo Go robotaxi fleet.
profile.category: Search / internet conglomerate plus full-stack AI cloud and foundation-model vendor — a mega-cap incumbent and, in the agent-memory market, more plausibly a competitor than a customer
profile.stage: Public company. NASDAQ IPO August 2005; secondary listing on HKEX in 2021.
profile.funding: Public — market-funded since its 2005 NASDAQ IPO; 2024 revenue CN¥133.1 billion (verified). Pre-IPO it raised modest venture rounds (roughly $12M total, including a 2004 round in which Google was an investor) — that pre-IPO detail is from prior knowledge and was NOT re-verified in this session. Venture 'funding' is not a meaningful field for this company.
profile.headcount_estimate: 35,900 (as of 2024) — verified via the Wikipedia infobox.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: none — not applicable; founded 2000 and NASDAQ-listed since 2005
profile.sells_to: Both, at massive scale. B2C: hundreds of millions of search and app users. B2B: advertisers (the revenue core), plus enterprise buyers of Baidu AI Cloud, Qianfan model services and Apollo automotive stacks. Developers: model APIs, agent-building tooling and open-source SDKs.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Baidu is a first-party builder and vendor of agent infrastructure, not a consumer of third-party agent tooling. VERIFIED in this session: Baidu released ERNIE 4.5 (foundation model) and ERNIE X1 (reasoning model) in March 2025, following ERNIE Bot (August 2023) and ERNIE 4.0 (October 2023); and the official baidu/cosui open-source repo (93 stars) is described as 'a frontend UI solution for the AI era... UI protocols, rendering SDKs, and component libraries for Generative UI, AI Agents, and LLM-powered applications' — i.e. Baidu ships an agent-interface layer as a product. FROM PRIOR KNOWLEDGE, not re-verified this session: the Qianfan platform's AgentBuilder / app-builder low-code agent tooling on Baidu AI Cloud, the Comate coding assistant, and the Xinxiang consumer general-agent app launched in 2025. Treat those product names as unconfirmed.
profile.why_they_need_memory: The stated need — agents that persist context across sessions instead of relearning every run — maps onto Baidu's consumer assistant and enterprise agent-platform ambitions. But Baidu sells the layer cognee sells: a company shipping its own foundation models, agent platform and agent UI protocol builds memory in-house and would more likely compete with cognee than buy it. As with Alipay, the citation is cognee's 'Trusted by engineers from' marquee (aria-label: 'Companies with engineers using cognee'), which is explicitly an individual-engineer adoption claim. The plausible truth is that a Baidu engineer used the open-source package. There is no evidence of a commercial relationship, and cognee's own named references are all small startups (Knowunity, SlideSpeak, Dynamo, Luccid, DeepMetis) plus a university researcher — which is the actual buyer profile for this category.
profile.confidence: high that Baidu is a real company and that the headcount, revenue, founding and ERNIE facts above are accurate (directly verified). LOW that Baidu is a cognee customer in any commercial sense — logo-wall-only evidence, no independent corroboration found. Pre-IPO funding detail is low-confidence.

profile.name: RapidSOS
profile.what_it_does: Operates what it calls 'the world's largest Safety Network' — an intelligent safety platform that pipes data from connected devices, apps and enterprises into 911 emergency communications centers (ECCs) and first responders. Core products: RapidSOS Unite (the interoperability platform for 911 centers — live video to 911, GIS mapping, drone deployment, analytics), RapidSOS Harmony AI (AI layer for ECCs), RapidSOS Connect (emergency API), plus acquired business lines IamResponding (responder coordination), eDispatches (dispatch), Northern911 (Canadian/regional 911 services) and Total Response. Self-reported scale as of Nov 2025: 1B+ emergencies supported, 600M+ connected devices and sensors, 5,800+ public-safety software integrations, 22,000+ federal/state/local public safety agencies, 200+ global enterprises including half of the US Fortune 10, 1M+ first responder users, >99% US population coverage. Device/app partners include Apple, Google, Uber, Axon, SimpliSafe, SiriusXM.
profile.category: Public safety / emergency response infrastructure and data platform (govtech + enterprise safety). AI-forward but not AI-native.
profile.stage: Late-stage private growth company (post-Series C, effectively Series D+). Founded 2012 and still private after 13+ years — a long-cycle infrastructure company, not a fast-cycle AI startup.
profile.funding: $450M+ total raised (company-stated, 18 Nov 2025). Verified round history: $14M Series A; $30M Series B (Nov 2018, Playground Global); $55M Series B completion (Oct 2019, Energy Impact Partners); $21M (2020, pandemic-related); $85M Series C (Feb 2021, Insight Partners); $75M Series C extension (Oct 2022, NightDragon); $150M round announced 5 March 2024 led by funds managed by BlackRock with NightDragon, Insight Partners, BAM Elevate, Manhattan Venture Partners, Acrew Capital and Harmonic Growth Partners; $100M announced 18 Nov 2025 with Apax Digital leading, bringing the total past $450M. Also took a strategic investment from Honeywell. Valuation: NOT disclosed in any round announcement — unknown, do not assume.
profile.headcount_estimate: unknown — RapidSOS does not publish a headcount; its careers page says only 'we're growing rapidly' and discloses no numbers. Given $450M raised, four acquired business units and 22,000+ agency customers, a few hundred employees is plausible, but I could not verify a figure and LinkedIn was not accessible in this session. Record as unknown rather than estimated.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company. Traditional VC-backed (Playground Global, Energy Impact Partners, Insight Partners, NightDragon, BlackRock, Apax Digital); founded out of Harvard/MIT (Michael Martin was at Harvard Business School, Nicholas Horelik at MIT).
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise and B2G/public sector. Three distinct motions: (1) government — 911 ECCs, fire/EMS, law enforcement, state agencies; (2) enterprise — healthcare, schools, autonomous vehicles, rideshare/delivery, critical infrastructure, retail, logistics; (3) device/platform partners (Apple, Google) reaching consumers indirectly. Enterprise and government sales cycles, not self-serve.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Two separate places. IN PRODUCT: Harmony AI, marketed as 'the first AI copilot for 911' — real-time call transcription and automatic translation into RapidSOS Unite, automated summaries of each 911 call's critical details, automated handling of non-emergency 10-digit lines with routing of service requests into CAD, and natural-language querying over incident data. There is also a separate 'AI Assistant' for automated call handling, and Harmony now runs on AT&T's ESInet. Notably this is deliberately copilot-shaped, not autonomous — telecommunicators retain decision authority, which is the correct posture for life-safety. INTERNALLY (the reason they appear on Coworker's wall): the Revenue Operations team uses Coworker/OM2 as a cross-system answer layer. Anna Waring, Director of Revenue Operations and Systems, describes the pre-Coworker state as 'hours stitching together Salesforce, Slack, and meeting notes to trust an answer.' So the agent buyer here is RevOps, not the AI product team.
profile.why_they_need_memory: The stated pain is exactly the agent-memory thesis: the answer to a business question lives distributed across Salesforce, Slack and meeting notes, and goes stale fast ('keeping up with how fast the business moves'). Structurally this company is unusually fragmented — four acquired product lines (IamResponding, eDispatches, Northern911, Total Response) each bringing their own systems and customer records, two very different GTM motions (public-sector agencies vs Fortune 10 enterprises), 22,000+ agency accounts, and a decade-plus of accumulated deal and integration history. A retrieval-only tool fails here because correctness requires knowing which of several overlapping systems is currently authoritative; the quote's emphasis is on the answer being 'current and correct' the moment it's asked, i.e. maintained state, not search.
sources: Coworker.ai OM2 launch post (content supplied in task brief; coworker.ai unreachable during research — vendor claims UNVERIFIED by me)

profile.name: Harness
profile.what_it_does: Enterprise software delivery platform, now marketed as an 'Autonomous SDLC' platform. Originally a CI/CD and continuous delivery company; today it spans pipelines, feature flags (via the Split.io acquisition), cloud cost management, security testing and runtime/API protection. Self-reported scale: 5.7M deployments/month, 1.5T+ feature-flag evaluations/month, 250B+ API calls protected/month, 1,000+ enterprise customers. Named customers include Citi, United Airlines, Workday, Experian, ADP and Morningstar. Compliance posture: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR. Founded and led by Jyoti Bansal, who previously founded AppDynamics (acquired by Cisco for $3.7B in 2017), co-founded Traceable (API security), and co-founded Unusual Ventures; Harness was spun out of his BIG Labs studio.
profile.category: DevOps / software delivery platform (CI/CD, feature flags, FinOps, AppSec) — repositioned around AI agents. Sells to developers and platform engineering.
profile.stage: Late-stage private, venture-backed (Series D/E+ territory). Founded 2017, still private.
profile.funding: $570M total raised (stated on Harness's own company page). Investors: Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Google Ventures (GV), Battery Ventures, Norwest Venture Partners, Citi Ventures, IVP, Alkeon Capital, Menlo Ventures, Sorenson Capital, Thomvest Ventures, Unusual Ventures, ServiceNow Ventures, BIG Labs. Valuation: unknown — not disclosed on the company's site and not verified in this research (a ~$3.7B figure has been reported publicly for an earlier round, but I could not confirm it here, so treat as unverified). ARR not disclosed. Harness has been acquisitive (Split.io, Traceable, Propelo are commonly cited) but the company page did not confirm acquisition details, so treat specific acquisition terms as unverified.
profile.headcount_estimate: 1,200+ worldwide (stated directly on Harness's company page), across 23 offices on five continents. Confidence high. Comfortably the largest of these three by headcount.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None — not a YC company. Spun out of BIG Labs, Jyoti Bansal's own venture studio, and funded by traditional growth VCs. Founder-brand company rather than accelerator-launched.
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise — specifically developers, DevOps and platform engineering teams inside large regulated enterprises (banking, airlines, HR/payroll, credit). Top-down enterprise sales with a free-trial motion underneath. Not SMB.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product as currently positioned. Harness ships four named AI agents: (1) Software Delivery Agent — builds and runs pipelines from commit to production using AI reasoning instead of hand-written scripts; (2) Security Testing Agent — triages real vulnerabilities and supply-chain risk, cutting false positives; (3) Runtime Protection Agent — defends APIs, applications and other AI agents at runtime; (4) Cost Management Agent — attributes AI and cloud spend by team and model. The governance layer is the differentiated part and the most relevant signal for this category: three configurable levels of autonomy from human-in-the-loop to fully autonomous execution within policy guardrails, Policy-as-Code (OPA) for AI governance, and full audit trails of every AI decision. Separately, Harness is itself a Coworker/OM2 production customer — named in the OM2 launch post alongside RapidSOS, Harri and Column — but with no quote and no named champion, so the internal use case is unknown.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two reinforcing reasons. First, as a buyer: 1,200+ employees across 23 offices and 1,000+ enterprise accounts, with a product surface assembled partly through acquisitions — internal answers span many tools and org boundaries, the same fragmentation pattern as RapidSOS. Second, and more strategically interesting: Harness builds long-running autonomous agents that operate on production systems under policy guardrails and must produce audit trails. That workload is fundamentally stateful — an agent executing across a multi-stage delivery pipeline needs durable memory of prior decisions, environment state and policy context, and the audit-trail requirement makes that memory a compliance artifact rather than a convenience. So Harness is simultaneously a customer of the category and a sophisticated evaluator of it, which is why its logo carries disproportionate credibility on an agent-memory vendor's wall.

profile.name: Harri
profile.what_it_does: Vertical HCM / frontline workforce-management platform for hospitality — restaurants (QSR, fast-casual, full-service), hotels, grocery and care operators. Positions itself as "The AI-First Workforce OS." Four product pillars: Talent Acquisition (branded career sites, job distribution, ATS, onboarding — 7.2M applications processed), Workforce Management (demand forecasting, scheduling, time & attendance), CoreHR, and Employee Engagement (comms, sentiment, recognition, instant pay). The differentiated piece is a labor-compliance engine covering Fair Workweek, break violations, minor-hour limits and Access-to-Hours provisions, with automatic audit trails for premium payments and good-faith documentation. Integrates with ADP, Paylocity, isolved and Workday for payroll. Self-reported scale: 55-60K customer locations, 5-6M users on the platform, 600+ clients, and "6 of the 10 largest hospitality brands." Named customers on-site include McDonald's US, Carl's Jr., Jersey Mike's, Dave's Hot Chicken and multi-unit Wendy's operators. Offices: New York HQ (NoHo/Bond St), London (70+), Ramallah, Palestine (170+ engineering/product), Hyderabad, India (deployment/payroll/analytics).
profile.category: Vertical HR tech / hospitality HCM + workforce management SaaS (frontline labor ops, scheduling, compliance)
profile.stage: Late-stage private / growth-stage. Not a conventional VC ladder — the disclosed investor set mixes a strategic corporate VC (ADP Ventures) with credit and specialty-finance funds (Golub Capital, Atalaya Capital Management), suggesting debt and structured financing rather than priced equity rounds. Most recent instrument reported is a small convertible note.
profile.funding: ~$76M total raised per CB Insights. Reported investors: ADP Ventures, Golub Capital, Atalaya Capital Management, NRD Capital, Metropolis Ventures, plus ~7 unnamed others. Latest reported instrument: a $3M convertible note (CB Insights placed it ~2 months before a September 2026 fetch, i.e. roughly July 2026). Treat the $76M as a single-source figure — Crunchbase returned 403 and Harri's own site has no press or investor page (harri.com/sitemap.xml has only 37 URLs and contains no /press, /news or /careers), so I could not cross-check it.
profile.headcount_estimate: Uncertain, roughly 400-700. TheOrg lists a 201-500 band, but Harri's own about-us page states 170+ engineering/product staff in Ramallah and 70+ in London alone, on top of the New York HQ and the Hyderabad delivery center — so the true figure is likely at or above the top of that band. No job board was reachable (Ashby, Greenhouse and Lever all returned 404 for 'harri'), and the LinkedIn company page could not be fetched (WebFetch returned an unrelated 1-person 'Harri' entity).
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None found. No YC, Techstars or accelerator affiliation appears on the site or in any source retrieved.
profile.founded_year: 2012 (per CB Insights). Founder Luke Fryer's origin story on the site — "our founder opened the first Burger King in Australia at the age of 22" — is consistent with a hospitality-operator-turned-software-founder, not a technical AI founder.
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise. Multi-unit and multi-brand hospitality operators, from single locations up to 500+ unit portfolios, sold to restaurant execs, franchisees and hotel/grocery/care groups. The buyer is an operations or HR leader, not a developer.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Harri ships "Salli," marketed as "hospitality's first and only end-to-end agentic AI platform" and explicitly positioned against the category norm — the homepage says "It's not a chatbot. It's not a copilot. It's a suite of autonomous AI agents that serves as a system of action." Salli is the single manager-facing assistant that orchestrates specialized background agents and "returns one clean response." Concrete agent behaviors advertised: Talent Gap Alert (detects understaffing and recommends pre-screened candidates), Compliance Warning (flags break violations and minor-hour-limit risk before penalties accrue), Overtime Cost Alert (projects labor cost in real time and proposes scheduling moves), Scheduling Optimization (one-click conflict resolution with consent/premium logging), Labor Insight (surfaces Fair Workweek rules at the point of scheduling), and Recognition Alert. Status is pre-GA — the Agentic AI page has a "Join The Waitlist" CTA and links a post titled "Harri Announces The Launch Of Its Agentic AI Open Beta." A customer quote from Kevin Brennan (Owner/Director of Operations, JMB Foods) describes it blocking non-compliant schedule posts and using historical sales data to optimize labor targets. Separately, Harri is itself a buyer: Coworker names it as a production OM2 customer, but gives no detail on whether OM2 sits inside Harri's product or is used internally.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pressures. (1) Product-side: their agents have to reason over deeply fragmented per-location operational state — schedules, time cards, sales forecasts, employee availability and history, and compliance rules that differ by state, city and jurisdiction — across 55-60K locations and millions of users. That is exactly the multi-hop, permission-scoped retrieval problem an organizational-memory layer claims to solve, and it is why an agent that starts cold each session is useless to a restaurant GM. (2) Internal: Harri is a ~15-year-old company running four offices across four time zones (New York, London, Ramallah, Hyderabad) with engineering separated from GTM by 7+ hours, so institutional context is scattered across Slack, CRM and docs. Coworker's OM2 post does not say which of these two the deployment serves, so the specific internal use case is unverified.
profile.confidence: high on identity, product and the agentic-AI positioning (all read directly off harri.com); medium on funding and headcount (single-source, no cross-check possible with web search exhausted)

profile.name: Upbound
profile.what_it_does: Commercial company behind Crossplane, the CNCF-graduated open-source framework for building Kubernetes-style control planes over cloud infrastructure. Upbound sells the enterprise product on top: managed/hosted control planes, an upgraded and supported Crossplane distribution with no-downtime migrations, Insights (drift and health analysis across resources), and as of Upbound v3 (Aug 2026) a 'Hub' that gives one API, one view and one governance model across every control plane an org runs, with central indexing and search. Target buyer is the platform-engineering team that wants to hand developers a self-service infrastructure API. Freemium: free tier plus enterprise pricing and support. Claims 1,000+ teams and 100M+ Crossplane downloads.
profile.category: dev tools / platform engineering / cloud infrastructure control planes
profile.stage: Series B (last announced round Nov 2021; no later round found)
profile.funding: $69M total per LinkedIn. Confirmed rounds: $9M Series A (May 2018, TechCrunch) and $60M Series B (Nov 2021, TechCrunch). Named investors: GV (Google Ventures), Altimeter Capital, Intel Capital. Series B lead not confirmed from a primary source - the TechCrunch article URL 404'd on fetch and only the search-listing headline was readable.
profile.headcount_estimate: 51-200 (LinkedIn band); globally distributed, remote-first, no offices named. Careers page currently shows no open roles, which suggests they are at the flat/lean end of that band.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: none - traditional VC path; the company is the commercial spinout of the Rook/Crossplane open-source lineage
profile.founded_year: 2017 (LinkedIn). Founder/CEO Bassam Tabbara, previously founder of Rook (the CNCF storage project) and an early Kubernetes-ecosystem figure.
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise, sold to platform engineering and infrastructure teams; developer-led adoption through open-source Crossplane
profile.how_they_use_agents: Agents are central to the current product positioning, not just internal tooling. The homepage tagline is 'Humans govern. Agents consume. Machines execute.' The platform page states that engineers and AI agents work through one API and one view, and that Hub's central index gives 'agents a single access point to your infrastructure' under the same governance and policy path a human operation takes. Marketing calls Crossplane 2.0 'The AI-Native Control Plane for the Agentic Era' (Aug 2025). Internally they are heavy AI-coding users: the blog has a CEO post 'Anthropic is subsidizing our AI coding at 13x. How long will it last?' (Jul 2026) and 'Converting Monolithic Crossplane Providers to Family Scoped Providers With Claude' (Oct 2025). No MCP server was mentioned on the platform or blog pages fetched.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. Internally: a small, fully remote team running a large open-source project plus an enterprise product, with knowledge spread across GitHub issues, Slack, docs and customer threads - classic company-brain territory, and they already run AI coding agents at volume. Strategically: their whole pitch is that agents will act on infrastructure and need a governed, indexed view of what exists; a company that sells 'context and governance for agents on infra' is a natural early adopter of 'context and governance for agents on company knowledge.' The Coworker citation is logo-only, so the specific internal use case is unconfirmed.

profile.name: Truecaller
profile.what_it_does: Global caller-ID, spam-blocking and communication-trust platform. The consumer app identifies unknown numbers, blocks spam and scam calls and SMS, and offers call recording, messaging and fraud protection; on iOS 18.2+ it gained real-time caller ID and spam blocking (Jan 2025). Over 500M monthly users, roughly 350M of them in India. Monetization is a three-way mix: ads in the free app, consumer Premium/Family subscriptions, and Truecaller for Business (verified business caller ID, enterprise messaging and call verification). Operated by True Software Scandinavia AB.
profile.category: consumer mobile app / communications trust and identity, plus B2B enterprise verified-communications
profile.stage: public company - listed on Nasdaq Stockholm since October 2021
profile.funding: Publicly listed; venture history before IPO: $1.3M from OpenOcean (Sept 2012), $18.8M from Sequoia Capital (Feb 2014), $60M from Atomico and Kleiner Perkins (Oct 2014), then IPO on Nasdaq Stockholm in 2021. Current revenue and market cap could not be confirmed - truecaller.com and investors.truecaller.com were both unfetchable in this session. Wikipedia notes a ~39% constant-currency revenue increase in 2025; treat that as secondhand.
profile.headcount_estimate: 201-500 (LinkedIn band). Majority of staff are in India (Bangalore/Gurgaon) despite the Stockholm HQ. By far the largest of the three companies here.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: none - founded in Sweden in 2009, traditional VC then IPO
profile.founded_year: 2009, by Alan Mamedi and Nami Zarringhalam; HQ Norrmalm, Stockholm, Sweden
profile.sells_to: prosumer/B2C (free ad-supported app plus Premium and Family subscriptions) and B2B enterprise (Truecaller for Business: banks, telcos, delivery and other high-call-volume brands buying verified business caller ID)
profile.how_they_use_agents: Product AI is real but is classifier/ML-shaped rather than agentic: large-scale spam and fraud scoring across a crowdsourced number graph, AI-based call screening and assistant features, and AI voice/deepfake scam detection. Wikipedia notes the company is 'expanding AI-based tools, subscriptions, and enterprise services.' I could not verify the specific 2026 AI feature set because truecaller.com and its investor site were both unreachable, and the Play Store page returned truncated content - so treat feature names with caution. The Coworker and Sana Labs citations are both internal-tooling signals, not product signals: Sana sells an AI knowledge assistant and learning platform, Coworker sells a company brain, and Truecaller is a Stockholm company like Sana.
profile.why_they_need_memory: The strongest structural case of the three. A 200-500 person public company split across Stockholm and India, serving 500M+ users, with regulatory and privacy obligations (an ongoing Swedish IMY/GDPR investigation as of Feb 2025), enterprise contracts and quarterly reporting duties. Knowledge is spread across time zones, functions and tooling, and a public company has real cost pressure on internal support and analytics work. That is the canonical buyer for an org-memory layer sitting over Slack, Jira, Salesforce and docs - and it is consistent with them also appearing on Sana's customer list.

profile.funding: Public — no venture funding relevant. Nasdaq: INTU, share price $332.70 as of Sept 4 2026 close (implying roughly $90B+ market cap). $7.2B cash and investments and $7.7B total debt as of July 31, 2026; issued $1.75B in notes in June 2026. FY2026 revenue $21.4B.
profile.headcount_estimate: 18,200 employees worldwide at end of fiscal year 2025 (stated directly on intuit.com 'Fast Facts'). FY2026 figure not published on the site at time of research; likely similar or modestly higher.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1983, long predates accelerators. Not a YC company.
profile.founded_year: 1983 (founded by Scott Cook and Tom Proulx)
profile.sells_to: Primarily B2B SMB (QuickBooks, Mailchimp) plus large-scale consumer/prosumer (TurboTax, Credit Karma), and increasingly B2B mid-market/enterprise via Intuit Enterprise Suite and its accountant channel (Lacerte, ProConnect, ProSeries, ProAdvisor).
profile.how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (1) In the product: CEO Sasan Goodarzi's FY26 earnings framing is that Intuit's strategy is 'to win as an AI-driven expert platform by creating a financial system of intelligence that increasingly does the work for consumers, businesses, and accountants' — i.e. agents that execute financial work, not just answer questions. Concretely verified: the Aug 31 2026 Perplexity partnership exposes QuickBooks and Mailchimp through MCP (Model Context Protocol) connectors inside Perplexity Computer, letting an external agent chase overdue invoices, set up recurring invoices, send payment links, retrieve payslips and payroll employee data, and track marketing campaign performance — all authenticated against the user's real QuickBooks/Mailchimp account. CTO Alex Balazs frames this as going 'from finding answers to getting personalized insights and taking decisive action.' Also shipped in 2026: conversational AI for mid-market CFOs and accounting firms (Aug 12, 2026 release), Mailchimp Analytics AI (May 28, 2026). Intuit's 'Big Bets' grew 34% and were 30% of FY26 revenue. (2) Internally: Intuit is a ~18K-person engineering-heavy org — the Glean use case is employee knowledge search across internal systems, not product embedding.
profile.why_they_need_memory: As a Glean buyer, the motivation is classic large-enterprise knowledge sprawl: 18,200 employees across 21 offices in 7 countries, five semi-independent product orgs (TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma, Mailchimp, Enterprise Suite) each with its own docs, wikis, tickets and Slack history, plus heavy compliance/regulatory documentation (money transmitter licensing, tax law, SOC/privacy). This is an IT/employee-productivity purchase — a search-and-retrieval layer over internal corpora — not a purchase of memory infrastructure for their shipped agents. Separately, their product-side agent work (MCP connectors executing financial actions against live books) does create genuine agent-state and audit requirements, but Intuit has the scale and security posture to build that in-house rather than buy it.

profile.name: Vanta
profile.what_it_does: Automated security compliance and GRC (governance, risk, compliance) platform. Vanta connects to 400+ tools in a customer's stack, continuously monitors controls, collects audit evidence, manages vendor/third-party risk, and drives companies to certification across 35+ frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI, etc.). Also sells Trust Center pages and security-questionnaire automation. Claims 16,000+ customers, named logos include Ramp, Cursor, Snowflake, Clay, GitHub, Duolingo, Intercom and Samsara.
profile.category: security compliance / GRC automation (B2B SaaS)
profile.stage: Series D (late-stage private)
profile.funding: ~$504M total disclosed. $3M seed 2018 (Y Combinator); $50M Series A May 2021 (Sequoia) at $500M; $110M Series B June 2022 (Craft Ventures) at $1.6B, plus a $40M extension Oct 2022; $150M Series C July 2024 (Sequoia) at $2.45B; $150M Series D July 2025 (Wellington Management) at $4.15B valuation.
profile.headcount_estimate: 1,000+ (as of April 2026, per Wikipedia). Offices in San Francisco, New York, Dublin, London, Sydney. LinkedIn blocked direct verification.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator — took a $3M seed via YC in 2018. Whether Vanta went through a formal YC batch (vs. YC simply investing) is unconfirmed.
profile.sells_to: B2B, full range — self-serve startups needing a first SOC 2, mid-market, and enterprise. Buyer is security/compliance/GRC leadership, often with the CTO or CISO. Not developer-led in the bottom-up sense, though the product is deeply technical.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Ships 'The Vanta AI Agent,' marketed as a '24/7 GRC engineering team.' It drafts security policies and compliance documentation, auto-completes inbound security questionnaires (claimed 95% answer-acceptance rate), verifies uploaded evidence and documentation, continuously monitors vendors' attack surfaces and alerts on issues, and generates personalized remediation snippets for Terraform, AWS CLI and CloudFormation. Separately branded 'Vanta AI' features automate compliance tasks and generate posture insights. The agent is a product feature sold to customers, not just internal tooling.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) Product: their agent's entire value depends on knowing one specific company's control set, written policies, prior questionnaire answers, auditor history and the live state of 400+ connected integrations — marketing copy literally says the agent knows 'your program inside and out.' That is a company-brain requirement, and stale or ungrounded context produces wrong compliance answers, which is a high-consequence failure. (2) Internal: 1,000+ employees across five offices in three continents, with security/legal/sales-engineering knowledge that has to be consistent — they buy Glean for enterprise search and Granola for meeting memory. Vanta appears on Glean's homepage logo wall and Granola's homepage logo wall.

profile.name: Figma
profile.what_it_does: Browser-based collaborative design platform — multiple people editing the same design file in real time — now expanded into a full product-development suite: Figma Design (core UI design/prototyping), Dev Mode (design-to-code handoff), FigJam (whiteboarding), Figma Slides, Figma Draw (vector illustration), Figma Sites (responsive site publishing), Figma Buzz (on-brand asset generation at scale), Figma Motion (animation), Figma Make (AI code generation from design) and Figma Weave (AI workflows for image, video and audio). Positions itself as 'the collaborative canvas for design, code, and AI.' Claims 95% of the Fortune 500 as users (March 2025), with Airbnb, Microsoft, Netflix, Stripe and Slack named.
profile.category: Design and collaboration SaaS, increasingly a developer-tools and AI-workflow company
profile.stage: Public. IPO'd July 31, 2025 on the NYSE under ticker FIG at $85/share.
profile.funding: Venture history: $3.8M seed (June 2013), $14M Series A (Dec 2015), $25M Series B (Feb 2018), $40M Series C (Feb 2019), $50M Series D (April 2020), $200M Series E (June 2021) — roughly $333M pre-IPO. Valuation path: $2B (2020), $10B (May 2021), $20B implied by Adobe's abandoned acquisition (Sept 2022), $8.3-9B by Dec 2023 after the deal collapsed. Post-IPO it spiked to a $56.3B market value, then fell to under $10B by June 2026; market cap was $12.86B at the Sept 4, 2026 close ($24.12/share, down ~61.5% year over year). 2025 revenue $1.06B with a $1.25B net loss (heavily IPO-related charges); TTM revenue $1.28B as of Sept 2026, growing 43-48% YoY with 85% gross margins.
profile.headcount_estimate: 1,886 employees (2025 figure, consistent across the IPO filing and current market data)
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Not YC. Dylan Field was a Thiel Fellow (2012), which funded him to drop out of Brown to start Figma — the closest thing to an accelerator in its history.
profile.founded_year: 2012 (Dylan Field and Evan Wallace, met studying CS at Brown; HQ in the Phelan Building, San Francisco; Field is chairman and CEO)
profile.sells_to: B2B, sold bottom-up: individual designers and product teams adopt it, then it expands to org-wide enterprise seats. Strong developer constituency via Dev Mode, Code Connect and its MCP server. Also has a genuine prosumer/individual free tier.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Figma is a heavy agent BUILDER, which makes it an unusual entry on a knowledge-vendor logo wall. Its design agent lives directly on the canvas and pulls context from four channels: uploaded files (user interviews, UX copy, data reports), pasted Figma file links (so it can read components, tokens, layouts and styles and reproduce existing design patterns), live web search, and MCP tool connectors to GitHub, Atlassian, Slack, Linear and Hex. It ships 'Skills' — saved prompts converted into slash commands that encode a team's creative direction and are shared across the team — plus generative plugins and shader tooling. Agent conversations are visible to file collaborators by default, deliberately, as 'a window into how someone thinks.' Code Connect feeds design-system knowledge to coding agents and cut token costs ~22.5% on average (Coinbase case study, Sept 2026). Figma also runs an official Figma MCP server. Separately cited as a customer by Guru, Notion AI and Granola — i.e. it buys internal-knowledge tooling for its own ~1,900-person org while building the design-context layer itself.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Figma has effectively concluded that context IS the product: their own framing is that the difference between an agent that speeds you up and one that understands how you work is context. Skills are a hand-rolled memory layer — reusable, shareable, team-scoped encoded judgment — and the MCP connectors plus Code Connect are a hand-rolled retrieval layer over design systems and adjacent tools. That makes them a validating reference for the category and simultaneously a hard sell: they built their own. Their internal need (a 1,900-person public company with ten-plus product lines shipped in about eighteen months) is the more straightforward buying motion, and is presumably what the Guru/Notion/Granola citations reflect.

profile.name: Ramp
profile.what_it_does: All-in-one financial operations / spend management platform for businesses. Corporate charge cards (Visa, unlimited physical and virtual, with per-vendor/category/amount controls and up to 5% cashback); expense management with receipt capture via SMS/Slack/mobile and automatic policy review; accounts payable (OCR invoice extraction, two- and three-way matching, zero domestic ACH fees); procurement and intake-to-pay (contract parsing, dynamic approval routing, auto-generated POs); corporate travel with policy enforcement at booking and automatic hotel rate re-shopping; and a treasury / FDIC-insured business account. Self-reported scale: 'Trusted by 70,000+ businesses', 27M+ hours saved, books closed 75% faster. HQ New York.
profile.category: B2B fintech / spend management and finance automation SaaS, now heavily agentic
profile.stage: Late-stage private (Series E and beyond)
profile.funding: ~$1.96B+ in disclosed equity, plus undisclosed rounds and large debt facilities. Rounds: ~$15M Series A (Feb 2020), $30M (Dec 2020), $115M Series B (Apr 2021), $300M Series C (Aug 2021), $300M Series D (Aug 2023), $150M Series D-2 (Jun 2024), undisclosed Series E (Jun 2025), undisclosed (Jul 2025), $300M led by Lightspeed (Nov 2025), $750M led by ICONIQ Growth (Jun 2026). Latest valuation $44B (Jun 2026).
profile.headcount_estimate: ~1,200-2,500. LinkedIn company page shows the 1,001-5,000 band and Wikipedia cites 1,200 for 2025; ~6,537 LinkedIn profiles associate with the name 'Ramp', which likely overcounts (name collisions / alumni). Treat 1,001-5,000 as the reliable range.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: Ramp itself did not go through an accelerator. Founders Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh previously built Paribus, a Y Combinator-backed startup acquired by Capital One in 2016 - reported, not verified in this session.
profile.founded_year: 2019 (March 2019; LinkedIn also lists Founded 2019). Founders: Eric Glyman (CEO), Karim Atiyeh (CTO), Gene Lee.
profile.sells_to: B2B across the full size range - startups and SMBs through mid-market and enterprise. Named customers on-site include Notion, Shopify, Webflow, Eventbrite, Poshmark and Quora.
profile.how_they_use_agents: 'Ramp Intelligence' is an AI layer embedded across the platform rather than a bolt-on. In accounts payable alone, 'four AI agents handle auto-coding, fraud prevention, approval routing, and automatic payment'. A named AI Policy Agent (shipped summer 2025) reviews 100% of expenses against company policy and escalates only exceptions. Other agentic surfaces: invoice transcription and line-item processing, three-way PO/receipt/invoice matching, contract parsing in procurement, real-time fraud and anomaly detection, duplicate-subscription flagging, vendor payment automation and cashback optimization, and automatic travel rate monitoring/rebooking. They claim 90% accurate auto-coding, learned from transaction patterns across 70,000+ customers. Explicit guardrail: 'no money ever moves without human confirmation' and 'all decisions transparent and auditable'.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two independent pulls. (1) PRODUCT SIDE - their agents are useless without durable per-tenant context, and their own marketing says so: agents are 'trained on your policy and controls', 'learn from past invoices', and 'learn from your company's spend patterns'. Coding an invoice or approving an expense correctly requires remembering this customer's chart of accounts, vendor history, approval chains, prior exceptions and reversals - that is agent memory, whether built or bought. (2) INTERNAL SIDE - a 1,000-5,000-person company compounding at this rate has a severe onboarding and single-source-of-truth problem across sales, support, finance and compliance, which is the classic Guru buy. Notably Ramp appears as a cited customer of Guru, Onyx (formerly Danswer), Notion AI and Granola simultaneously, which suggests they buy context/knowledge tooling broadly across the stack rather than standardizing on one - a positive signal for category demand but a crowded competitive field, and a hint they are also a favourite logo for vendors to cite.

profile.name: Netlify
profile.what_it_does: Netlify is a web development and application delivery platform — the company that popularized the 'Jamstack' term. It lets teams build, deploy and scale web apps and sites from Git, CLI, drag-and-drop, or (as of the current site) an AI prompt. The platform bundles a global CDN with 99.99% claimed uptime, atomic deploys and deploy previews for every change, serverless functions and APIs, managed databases, file/blob storage, and built-in authentication. Positioning has shifted materially toward AI: the homepage headline is 'Create with AI or code, deploy instantly on production infrastructure,' and it now advertises Agent Runners (prototype and ship AI features / run coding agents including Claude and Codex) and an AI Gateway that connects apps to major model providers. Claims 10M+ developers and 60M+ apps deployed.
profile.category: developer tools / frontend cloud and web application PaaS; increasingly an AI app-building and agent-hosting platform

Investors named by the company: Andreessen Horowitz, Bessemer Venture Partners, Bloomberg Beta, BOND, Designer Fund, EQT Ventures, Kleiner Perkins, Mango Capital, Menlo Ventures, and at.inc/, plus angels from Figma, GitHub, Heroku, Rackspace, Slack and Yelp. profile.sells_to: Both developers (large PLG self-serve base, free tier, 10M+ developers) and enterprise (thousands of enterprises; logo wall includes Meta, Autodesk, Zscaler, Stack Overflow, Riot Games, Kubernetes and Figma). The buying motion spans individual devs up through enterprise platform teams, with collaboration framed around marketers, designers, engineers, ops and product.
profile.how_they_use_agents: Netlify is now a host and runtime for other people's agents rather than an operator of internal-facing agents. Agent Runners let users prototype and ship AI features and run coding agents (Claude and Codex are named) that build and deploy apps — 'Describe what you want to build. An AI agent handles the rest.' The AI Gateway is a managed pathway from a deployed app to major model providers. So the agent surface is infrastructure-level: agents as a build input (prompt-to-deploy) and agents as a workload their customers run on Netlify.

Treat as a probable-but-unverified logo placement. If real, the plausible rationale: Netlify sits on enormous build, deploy and edge-traffic telemetry across 60M+ apps, and would want internal teams (and possibly enterprise customers) to query usage, build performance and account health in natural language without a data team hand-building every report — the same embedded/self-serve analytics pattern as DealHub. A secondary angle: agent-built apps need durable project context, which is adjacent to the agent-memory category, but nothing on Netlify's site indicates they buy that externally.

profile.name: DoubleVerify
profile.what_it_does: DoubleVerify (NYSE: DV) is a digital advertising verification and media-effectiveness company. Its DV Media AdVantage Platform (DV MAP) organizes around three functions: Verify (measure media quality — ad fraud and invalid traffic detection, viewability, brand safety and suitability, content context, attention — across open web, social, CTV/streaming, and commerce/retail media), Optimize (AI-driven bidding algorithms that dynamically improve campaign performance, built largely on the 2023 Scibids acquisition), and Prove (attribution, marketing mix modeling and incrementality, built largely on the 2025 Rockerbox acquisition). Product names include DV Authentic Ad, DV Authentic Attention, DV Publisher Suite and DV Pinnacle. The company says it analyzes over 8.3 trillion media transactions per year and optimizes 25 billion impressions monthly.
profile.category: adtech — ad verification, brand safety, media measurement and campaign optimization
profile.stage: Public company, and currently mid-acquisition. IPO'd on NYSE April 21, 2021 at $27.00/share. As of September 2026 it is under an announced all-cash acquisition by Nielsen at approximately $2.15B ($13.60 per share); the stock traded at $13.36 on Sept 4, 2026, essentially pinned to the deal price.
profile.funding: Public — not venture funded at this stage. 2025 revenue $748.29M (+13.9% YoY); TTM revenue $768.82M (+7.6%); 2025 net income $50.65M; market cap ~$2.07B. IPO April 2021 at $27/share. Pre-IPO private ownership (private equity majority stake and late-stage growth investment) was not verified in this session — do not quote a pre-IPO funding number. Acquisitions made: Scibids (2023), Rockerbox (2025).
profile.headcount_estimate: ~1,231 employees (stockanalysis.com company profile). Offices or commercial operations in 31 locations across 25 countries, including New York, Chicago, Berlin, Tokyo and Sydney. By far the largest of the three companies here.
profile.yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable. Founded 2008, long pre-dating the modern accelerator route for this category, and took a private-equity-then-IPO path.
profile.founded_year: 2008. Headquartered at 462 Broadway, New York, NY. CEO Mark Zagorski.
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise, three-sided: brands and agencies (Procter & Gamble, General Motors, FanDuel), holding companies and agency groups (WPP, IPG Mediabrands, Publicis Groupe), publishers, and retail-media marketplaces. Large-enterprise, procurement-heavy sales motion — the buyer is a CMO org, media-buying team or ad ops function.
profile.how_they_use_agents: DV Neura, announced June 17, 2026, is the company's 'cognitive engine' embedded across DV MAP. It is a hybrid of large language models, specialized ML and deterministic rules, used to interpret emerging topics and nuanced meaning across text, image, video and audio at scale (content classification expanded 300x since the start of 2026; 500M+ impressions blocked in low-quality environments since January 2026). Two named agents: the DV Neura Insight Agent, which surfaces campaign insights conversationally and — notably — exposes DV's verification and performance data to Claude, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and other assistants over MCP; and the DV Neura Activation Agent, slated for Q3 2026, which will autonomously execute approved campaign changes inside advertiser-defined guardrails. The strategic direction is letting advertisers query DV data from whatever assistant they already use rather than logging into a DV dashboard.
profile.why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: DoubleVerify's status as a Jedify customer is UNCONFIRMED. Like Netlify, it appears only as an uncaptioned homepage carousel logo (Group-625156.svg / logo02.svg), never named in text; my fetch of jedify.com's named-testimonial list did not include DoubleVerify. Treat as probable-but-unverified. If real, the fit is strong and specific: DV's whole 2026 strategy is exposing 8.3 trillion transactions' worth of measurement data to external LLM assistants via MCP, which only works if there is a semantic layer mapping DV's metric taxonomy (viewability, IVT, suitability tiers, attention, MFA classifications) onto business meaning — otherwise an agent hitting raw tables will produce confidently wrong campaign answers for a P&G or WPP. Add the embedded/multi-tenant angle: thousands of brand and agency customers each want their own campaign data queried conversationally, and DV cannot build a bespoke analytics surface per advertiser. profile.name: Qualcomm (Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.)
profile.what_it_does: Fabless semiconductor and wireless-technology giant. Designs Snapdragon SoCs (CPU/GPU/NPU/modem) for smartphones, PCs, XR, wearables and automotive; Dragonwing for industrial/IoT edge; Dragonfly for data-center AI inference. Two revenue engines: QCT, the chip business (~80% of revenue), and QTL, the CDMA/3G/4G/5G patent-licensing business (~19%). Founded July 1, 1985 in San Diego by Irwin Jacobs, Andrew Viterbi, Franklin Antonio and four others. FY2025 revenue $44.28B, operating income $12.36B, ~$180B market cap (NASDAQ: QCOM). Recent AI-driven M&A: Alphawave IP ($2.4B, June 2025), Arduino (Oct 2025), Modular ($3.9B, 2026).
profile.category: semiconductors / edge AI silicon — NOT an agent-memory buyer; this is a platform/silicon partnership
profile.stage: Public company (NASDAQ: QCOM), IPO December 1991
profile.funding: N/A — public since 1991. FY2025 revenue $44.28B, net income $5.54B, market cap ~$180B
profile.headcount_estimate: ~52,000 (2025); 170 offices in 30+ countries
profile.yc_or_accelerator: none
profile.sells_to: B2B enterprise — device OEMs, automakers, carriers, industrial/IoT customers; plus developers via Qualcomm AI Hub
profile.how_they_use_agents: Qualcomm sells the substrate agents run on, rather than running agents as its own product. Qualcomm AI Hub offers hundreds of pre-optimized ML models, SLMs and LLMs for on-device deployment, with tooling (AIMET quantization, ONNX Runtime, ExecuTorch, LiteRT) to profile/test/deploy across 60+ cloud-hosted device targets. Marketing explicitly foregrounds 'agentic AI': agentic IT ticket automation, multi-device orchestration, voice interfaces, web-research workflows. Copilot+ PCs on Snapdragon X-series, and the Snapdragon X2 Elite, are positioned as agentic-AI hosts. The 2026 Modular acquisition ($3.9B) buys edge-to-cloud AI infrastructure. Qualcomm sized edge gen-AI at a $900B TAM by 2030.
profile.why_they_need_memory: They do not buy agent memory — they want it as a workload. The Memories.ai relationship is inverted relative to a customer relationship: Memories.ai announced it will 'run natively on Qualcomm processors starting in 2026,' i.e. Memories.ai is porting to Qualcomm silicon, and Qualcomm's Vinesh Sukumar (VP Product Management, Head of Gen AI/ML) gave a supporting quote about combining Qualcomm edge computing with the Large Visual Memory Model. Confirmed independently: memories.ai's 'Project LUCI' post (June 1, 2026) names the Qualcomm X2 Elite as the desktop compute platform and Snapdragon AR Glasses as the wearable capture device, running a 3B-parameter embedding model 100% on-device via Windows ML. Qualcomm's strategic interest is that persistent on-device visual memory is a heavy, sticky NPU workload that justifies premium silicon and differentiates edge inference against cloud. Treat Qualcomm as an ecosystem enabler / co-marketing partner, not as a buyer of the category.

profile.name: Ring (Amazon)
profile.what_it_does: Consumer and small-business home-security hardware plus subscription software, owned by Amazon. Product lines: video doorbells (wired, battery, 4K Pro), outdoor cameras (Floodlight Cam Plus, Spotlight Cam 2K, Outdoor Cam Plus), indoor cameras (Pan-Tilt), alarm kits and contact sensors, chimes and accessories, and professional installation from $129.99. HQ Santa Monica, California.

profile.stage: Wholly-owned Amazon subsidiary since April 2018 (previously VC-backed)
profile.funding: Acquired by Amazon April 12, 2018 for ~$839M (some sources say ~$1.15B). Pre-acquisition VC rounds existed but I could not verify totals this session — treat as unknown.
profile.headcount_estimate: ~1,300 as of 2018; current headcount unknown — Amazon does not break Ring out separately
profile.yc_or_accelerator: none
profile.sells_to: Consumer / prosumer households, plus B2B SMB via Ring for Business; and now third-party developers via the Ring Appstore
profile.how_they_use_agents: Ring ships first-party AI directly in the product: 'Video Descriptions' generate text explanations of what triggered a motion alert; 'Familiar Faces' (launched Sept 2025) does opt-in face recognition to suppress noise notifications; 'Search Party' (Oct 2025) uses object recognition across the Neighbors network to find lost pets; 'Active Warnings' produce automatic spoken alerts. Strategically more important: Ring has opened a developer platform — the Ring Appstore, live at ring.com/appstore in limited availability, framed as turning 'Ring data into actionable intelligence,' with launch categories for business intelligence and operations, home analytics, elderly care monitoring, and pet wellness. That is Ring exposing its camera fleet as a substrate for third-party AI apps.
profile.why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE PREMISE: Ring is not buying agent memory from Memories.ai — the direction is the reverse. Memories.ai's own post states 'Memories.ai is now available in the Ring Appstore, bringing our visual memory technology to Ring cameras used in homes and businesses around the world' (authored by Shawn Shen, Memories.ai co-founder/CEO). There are no quotes from any Ring or Amazon employee in that post, and memories.ai is not named on the public Ring Appstore page. Memories.ai's homepage stat '100M+ cameras powered by partner integrations' is derived from Ring's installed base, not from a Ring purchase order. TechCrunch coverage of the Ring app-store launch listed memories.ai as one launch app, a risk/security detection app for fires, smoke, falls and leaks. Ring does have the exact problem the category solves — continuous video that must become searchable, persistent, pattern-aware memory rather than raw clips — but it builds that in-house (Video Descriptions, Familiar Faces) and lets third parties fill gaps through the app store. As a go-to-market signal, Ring is a distribution channel, not an ICP.

profile.yc_or_accelerator: none

profile.how_they_use_agents: Product-side: AI DJ (personalized, now takes real-time voice requests in 60+ markets and via Android Auto), AI Playlist (natural-language prompt-to-playlist, with iterative refinement like 'more upbeat', now in 40+ additional markets), audiobook Recaps, and AI-provenance tooling (AI persona badges, AI credits, SongDNA, Verified by Spotify). Spotify has also exposed itself as a connected tool for third-party assistants - users can link their account to Claude and to ChatGPT for taste- and history-based recommendations, which makes Spotify a target surface for external agents rather than only an agent builder. Internal/ops side: Spotify appears on Guru's customer logo wall (asset '2025_Solutions_Customer_Spotify.svg' and the /customers marquee), i.e. as a buyer of an AI knowledge layer for internal teams - logo only, no quote, so the internal deployment scope is unverified.
profile.why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) Consumer-product memory: every marquee AI feature (DJ, AI Playlist, external assistant integrations) is worthless without long-horizon listening history and taste state - personalization IS memory for them, though they build that in-house rather than buying it. (2) Org memory: ~7,300 employees across Stockholm/NYC/global offices in a famously autonomous 'squad' structure means internal knowledge is heavily fragmented across teams and tools; that is the classic Guru buying motive - support, sales enablement, and internal ops needing one verified answer instead of tribal knowledge. As a buyer they are the 'large, non-AI-native enterprise with knowledge sprawl' archetype, not the 'AI startup wiring memory into its agent' archetype.
